 # When to implement `From`
O While there's no technical restrictions on which conversions can be done using
I a `From` implementation, the general expectation is that the conversions
+ should typically be restricted as follows:
N * The conversion is *infallible*: if the conversion can fail, use [`TryFrom`]
4   instead; don't provide a `From` impl that panics.
L * The conversion is *lossless*: semantically, it should not lose or discard
H   information. For example, `i32: From<u16>` exists, where the original
N   value can be recovered using `u16: TryFrom<i32>`.  And `String: From<&str>`
K   exists, where you can get something equivalent to the original value via
L   `Deref`.  But `From` cannot be used to convert from `u32` to `u16`, since
M   that cannot succeed in a lossless way.  (There's some wiggle room here for
B   information not considered semantically relevant.  For example,
N   `Box<[T]>: From<Vec<T>>` exists even though it might not preserve capacity,
C   like how two vectors can be equal despite differing capacities.)
K * The conversion is *value-preserving*: the conceptual kind and meaning of
K   the resulting value is the same, even though the Rust type and technical
O   representation might be different.  For example `-1_i8 as u8` is *lossless*,
N   since `as` casting back can recover the original value, but that conversion
P   is *not* available via `From` because `-1` and `255` are different conceptual
B   values (despite being identical bit patterns technically).  But
Q   `f32: From<i16>` *is* available because `1_i16` and `1.0_f32` are conceptually
Q   the same real number (despite having very different bit patterns technically).
E   `String: From<char>` is available because they're both *text*, but
I   `String: From<u32>` is *not* available, since `1` (a number) and `"1"`
K   (text) are too different.  (Converting values to text is instead covered
2   by the [`Display`](crate::fmt::Display) trait.)
K * The conversion is *obvious*: it's the only reasonable conversion between
H   the two types.  Otherwise it's better to have it be a named method or
L   constructor, like how [`str::as_bytes`] is a method and how integers have
C   methods like [`u32::from_ne_bytes`], [`u32::from_le_bytes`], and
M   [`u32::from_be_bytes`], none of which are `From` implementations.  Whereas
P   there's only one reasonable way to wrap an [`Ipv6Addr`](crate::net::Ipv6Addr)
P   into an [`IpAddr`](crate::net::IpAddr), thus `IpAddr: From<Ipv6Addr>` exists.
$ [`String`] implements `From<&str>`:
E An explicit conversion from a `&str` to a String is done as follows:
" let string = "hello".to_string();
* let other_string = String::from("hello");
" assert_eq!(string, other_string);

.Interfaces for working with Errors.
# Error Handling In Rust
The Rust language provides two complementary systems for constructing /
representing, reporting, propagating, reacting to, and discarding errors.
These responsibilities are collectively known as "error handling." The
components of the first system, the panic runtime and interfaces, are most
commonly used to represent bugs that have been detected in your program. The
components of the second system, `Result`, the error traits, and user
defined types, are used to represent anticipated runtime failure modes of
your program.
## The Panic Interfaces
The following are the primary interfaces of the panic system and the
responsibilities they cover:
* [`panic!`] and [`panic_any`] (Constructing, Propagated automatically)
* [`set_hook`], [`take_hook`], and [`PanicHookInfo`] (Reporting)
* [`#[panic_handler]`][panic-handler] and [`PanicInfo`] (Reporting in no_std)
* [`catch_unwind`] and [`resume_unwind`] (Discarding, Propagating)
The following are the primary interfaces of the error system and the
responsibilities they cover:
* [`Result`] (Propagating, Reacting)
* The [`Error`] trait (Reporting)
* User defined types (Constructing / Representing)
* [`match`] and [`downcast`] (Reacting)
* The question mark operator ([`?`]) (Propagating)
* The partially stable [`Try`] traits (Propagating, Constructing)
* [`Termination`] (Reporting)
## Converting Errors into Panics
The panic and error systems are not entirely distinct. Often times errors
that are anticipated runtime failures in an API might instead represent bugs
to a caller. For these situations the standard library provides APIs for
constructing panics with an `Error` as its source.
* [`Result::unwrap`]
* [`Result::expect`]
These functions are equivalent, they either return the inner value if the
`Result` is `Ok` or panic if the `Result` is `Err` printing the inner error
as the source. The only difference between them is that with `expect` you
provide a panic error message to be printed alongside the source, whereas
`unwrap` has a default message indicating only that you unwrapped an `Err`.
Of the two, `expect` is generally preferred since its `msg` field allows you
to convey your intent and assumptions which makes tracking down the source
of a panic easier. `unwrap` on the other hand can still be a good fit in
situations where you can trivially show that a piece of code will never
panic, such as `"127.0.0.1".parse::<std::net::IpAddr>().unwrap()` or early
prototyping.
# Common Message Styles
There are two common styles for how people word `expect` messages. Using
the message to present information to users encountering a panic
("expect as error message") or using the message to present information
to developers debugging the panic ("expect as precondition").
In the former case the expect message is used to describe the error that
has occurred which is considered a bug. Consider the following example:
```should_panic
// Read environment variable, panic if it is not present
let path = std::env::var("IMPORTANT_PATH").unwrap();
In the "expect as error message" style we would use expect to describe
that the environment variable was not set when it should have been:
```should_panic
let path = std::env::var("IMPORTANT_PATH")
    .expect("env variable `IMPORTANT_PATH` is not set");
In the "expect as precondition" style, we would instead describe the
reason we _expect_ the `Result` should be `Ok`. With this style we would
prefer to write:
```should_panic
let path = std::env::var("IMPORTANT_PATH")
    .expect("env variable `IMPORTANT_PATH` should be set by `wrapper_script.sh`");
The "expect as error message" style does not work as well with the
default output of the std panic hooks, and often ends up repeating
information that is already communicated by the source error being
unwrapped:
```text
thread 'main' panicked at src/main.rs:4:6:
env variable `IMPORTANT_PATH` is not set: NotPresent
In this example we end up mentioning that an env variable is not set,
followed by our source message that says the env is not present, the
only additional information we're communicating is the name of the
environment variable being checked.
The "expect as precondition" style instead focuses on source code
readability, making it easier to understand what must have gone wrong in
situations where panics are being used to represent bugs exclusively.
Also, by framing our expect in terms of what "SHOULD" have happened to
prevent the source error, we end up introducing new information that is
independent from our source error.
```text
thread 'main' panicked at src/main.rs:4:6:
env variable `IMPORTANT_PATH` should be set by `wrapper_script.sh`: NotPresent
In this example we are communicating not only the name of the
environment variable that should have been set, but also an explanation
for why it should have been set, and we let the source error display as
a clear contradiction to our expectation.
**Hint**: If you're having trouble remembering how to phrase
expect-as-precondition style error messages remember to focus on the word
"should" as in "env variable should be set by blah" or "the given binary
should be available and executable by the current user".

_ `Request` supports generic, type-driven access to data. Its use is currently restricted to the
` standard library in cases where trait authors wish to allow trait implementors to share generic
Q information across trait boundaries. The motivating and prototypical use case is
T `core::error::Error` which would otherwise require a method per concrete type (e.g.
Q `std::backtrace::Backtrace` instance that implementors want to expose to users).
 # Data flow
\ To describe the intended data flow for Request objects, let's consider two conceptual users
 separated by API boundaries:
^ * Consumer - the consumer requests objects using a Request instance; e.g. a crate that offers
c   fancy `Error`/`Result` reporting to users wants to request a Backtrace from a given `dyn Error`.
^ * Producer - the producer provides objects when requested via Request; e.g. a library with an
]   an `Error` implementation that automatically captures backtraces at the time instances are
   created.
\ The consumer only needs to know where to submit their request and is expected to handle the
` request not being fulfilled by the use of `Option<T>` in the responses offered by the producer.
] * A Producer initializes the value of one of its fields of a specific type. (or is otherwise
K   prepared to generate a value requested). e.g., `backtrace::Backtrace` or
   `std::backtrace::Backtrace`.
] * A Consumer requests an object of a specific type (say `std::backtrace::Backtrace`). In the
b   case of a `dyn Error` trait object (the Producer), there are functions called `request_ref` and
I   `request_value` to simplify obtaining an `Option<T>` for a given type.
_ * The Producer, when requested, populates the given Request object which is given as a mutable
   reference.
] * The Consumer extracts a value or reference to the requested type from the `Request` object
]   wrapped in an `Option<T>`; in the case of `dyn Error` the aforementioned `request_ref` and
d   `request_value` methods mean that `dyn Error` users don't have to deal with the `Request` type at
\   all (but `Error` implementors do). The `None` case of the `Option` suggests only that the
f   Producer cannot currently offer an instance of the requested type, not that it can't or never will.
a The best way to demonstrate this is using an example implementation of `Error`'s `provide` trait

= Types whose values can be duplicated simply by copying bits.
> By default, variable bindings have 'move semantics.' In other
 words:
 struct Foo;
 let x = Foo;
 let y = x;
1 // `x` has moved into `y`, and so cannot be used
3 // println!("{x:?}"); // error: use of moved value
G However, if a type implements `Copy`, it instead has 'copy semantics':
L // We can derive a `Copy` implementation. `Clone` is also required, as it's
 // a supertrait of `Copy`.
 #[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone)]
 // `y` is a copy of `x`
 println!("{x:?}"); // A-OK!
V It's important to note that in these two examples, the only difference is whether you
W are allowed to access `x` after the assignment. Under the hood, both a copy and a move
V can result in bits being copied in memory, although this is sometimes optimized away.
 ## How can I implement `Copy`?
V There are two ways to implement `Copy` on your type. The simplest is to use `derive`:
4 You can also implement `Copy` and `Clone` manually:
 impl Copy for MyStruct { }
 impl Clone for MyStruct {
"     fn clone(&self) -> MyStruct {
\ There is a small difference between the two. The `derive` strategy will also place a `Copy`
 bound on type parameters:
 struct MyStruct<T>(T);
' impl<T: Copy> Copy for MyStruct<T> { }
] This isn't always desired. For example, shared references (`&T`) can be copied regardless of
] whether `T` is `Copy`. Likewise, a generic struct containing markers such as [`PhantomData`]
6 could potentially be duplicated with a bit-wise copy.
5 ## What's the difference between `Copy` and `Clone`?
X Copies happen implicitly, for example as part of an assignment `y = x`. The behavior of
A `Copy` is not overloadable; it is always a simple bit-wise copy.
P Cloning is an explicit action, `x.clone()`. The implementation of [`Clone`] can
V provide any type-specific behavior necessary to duplicate values safely. For example,
S the implementation of [`Clone`] for [`String`] needs to copy the pointed-to string
U buffer in the heap. A simple bitwise copy of [`String`] values would merely copy the
Z pointer, leading to a double free down the line. For this reason, [`String`] is [`Clone`]
 but not `Copy`.
W [`Clone`] is a supertrait of `Copy`, so everything which is `Copy` must also implement
^ [`Clone`]. If a type is `Copy` then its [`Clone`] implementation only needs to return `*self`
 (see the example above).
 ## When can my type be `Copy`?
Y A type can implement `Copy` if all of its components implement `Copy`. For example, this
 struct can be `Copy`:
 struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
[ A struct can be `Copy`, and [`i32`] is `Copy`, therefore `Point` is eligible to be `Copy`.
 By contrast, consider
 # struct Point;

     points: Vec<Point>,
X The struct `PointList` cannot implement `Copy`, because [`Vec<T>`] is not `Copy`. If we
? attempt to derive a `Copy` implementation, we'll get an error:
_ the trait `Copy` cannot be implemented for this type; field `points` does not implement `Copy`
V Shared references (`&T`) are also `Copy`, so a type can be `Copy`, even when it holds
U shared references of types `T` that are *not* `Copy`. Consider the following struct,
Y which can implement `Copy`, because it only holds a *shared reference* to our non-`Copy`
 type `PointList` from above:
 # struct PointList;

#     point_list_ref: &'a PointList,
# ## When *can't* my type be `Copy`?
Y Some types can't be copied safely. For example, copying `&mut T` would create an aliased
V mutable reference. Copying [`String`] would duplicate responsibility for managing the
/ [`String`]'s buffer, leading to a double free.
[ Generalizing the latter case, any type implementing [`Drop`] can't be `Copy`, because it's
? managing some resource besides its own [`size_of::<T>`] bytes.
\ If you try to implement `Copy` on a struct or enum containing non-`Copy` data, you will get
 the error [E0204].
& [E0204]: ../../error_codes/E0204.html
$ ## When *should* my type be `Copy`?
Z Generally speaking, if your type _can_ implement `Copy`, it should. Keep in mind, though,
Z that implementing `Copy` is part of the public API of your type. If the type might become
X non-`Copy` in the future, it could be prudent to omit the `Copy` implementation now, to
 avoid a breaking API change.

 # A ghastly note 
I Though they both have scary names, `PhantomData` and 'phantom types' are
F related, but not identical. A phantom type parameter is simply a type
J parameter which is never used. In Rust, this often causes the compiler to
L complain, and the solution is to add a "dummy" use by way of `PhantomData`.
 ## Unused lifetime parameters
K Perhaps the most common use case for `PhantomData` is a struct that has an
F unused lifetime parameter, typically as part of some unsafe code. For
L example, here is a struct `Slice` that has two pointers of type `*const T`,
- presumably pointing into an array somewhere:
 ```compile_fail,E0392
 struct Slice<'a, T> {
     start: *const T,
     end: *const T,
@ The intention is that the underlying data is only valid for the
A lifetime `'a`, so `Slice` should not outlive `'a`. However, this
@ intent is not expressed in the code, since there are no uses of
A the lifetime `'a` and hence it is not clear what data it applies
C to. We can correct this by telling the compiler to act *as if* the
. `Slice` struct contained a reference `&'a T`:
!     phantom: PhantomData<&'a T>,
@ This also in turn infers the lifetime bound `T: 'a`, indicating
= that any references in `T` are valid over the lifetime `'a`.
9 When initializing a `Slice` you simply provide the value
' `PhantomData` for the field `phantom`:
  # use std::marker::PhantomData;
 # struct Slice<'a, T> {
 #     start: *const T,
 #     end: *const T,
# #     phantom: PhantomData<&'a T>,
1 fn borrow_vec<T>(vec: &Vec<T>) -> Slice<'_, T> {
     let ptr = vec.as_ptr();
     Slice {
         start: ptr,
,         end: unsafe { ptr.add(vec.len()) },
         phantom: PhantomData,

 Overloadable operators.
D Implementing these traits allows you to overload certain operators.
K Some of these traits are imported by the prelude, so they are available in
K every Rust program. Only operators backed by traits can be overloaded. For
K example, the addition operator (`+`) can be overloaded through the [`Add`]
K trait, but since the assignment operator (`=`) has no backing trait, there
K is no way of overloading its semantics. Additionally, this module does not
K provide any mechanism to create new operators. If traitless overloading or
G custom operators are required, you should look toward macros to extend
 Rust's syntax.
C Implementations of operator traits should be unsurprising in their
> respective contexts, keeping in mind their usual meanings and
M [operator precedence]. For example, when implementing [`Mul`], the operation
C should have some resemblance to multiplication (and share expected
  properties like associativity).
F Note that the `&&` and `||` operators are currently not supported for
L overloading. Due to their short circuiting nature, they require a different
M design from traits for other operators like [`BitAnd`]. Designs for them are
 under discussion.
C Many of the operators take their operands by value. In non-generic
B contexts involving built-in types, this is usually not a problem.
> However, using these operators in generic code, requires some
J attention if values have to be reused as opposed to letting the operators
; consume them. One option is to occasionally use [`clone`].
E Another option is to rely on the types involved providing additional
I operator implementations for references. For example, for a user-defined
F type `T` which is supposed to support addition, it is probably a good
J idea to have both `T` and `&T` implement the traits [`Add<T>`][`Add`] and
K [`Add<&T>`][`Add`] so that generic code can be written without unnecessary
	 cloning.

 # Deref coercion
M If `T` implements `Deref<Target = U>`, and `v` is a value of type `T`, then:
J * In immutable contexts, `*v` (where `T` is neither a reference nor a raw
1   pointer) is equivalent to `*Deref::deref(&v)`.
9 * Values of type `&T` are coerced to values of type `&U`
K * `T` implicitly implements all the methods of the type `U` which take the
   `&self` receiver.
O For more details, visit [the chapter in *The Rust Programming Language*][book]
O as well as the reference sections on [the dereference operator][ref-deref-op],
+ [method resolution], and [type coercions].
* # When to implement `Deref` or `DerefMut`
G The same advice applies to both deref traits. In general, deref traits
 **should** be implemented if:
H 1. a value of the type transparently behaves like a value of the target
	    type;
: 1. the implementation of the deref function is cheap; and
K 1. users of the type will not be surprised by any deref coercion behavior.
; In general, deref traits **should not** be implemented if:
9 1. the deref implementations could fail unexpectedly; or
G 1. the type has methods that are likely to collide with methods on the
    target type; or
L 1. committing to deref coercion as part of the public API is not desirable.
G Note that there's a large difference between implementing deref traits
J generically over many target types, and doing so only for specific target
 types.
L Generic implementations, such as for [`Box<T>`][box] (which is generic over
K every type and dereferences to `T`) should be careful to provide few or no
K methods, since the target type is unknown and therefore every method could
B collide with one on the target type, causing confusion for users.
G `impl<T> Box<T>` has no methods (though several associated functions),
 partly for this reason.
H Specific implementations, such as for [`String`][string] (whose `Deref`
I implementation has `Target = str`) can have many methods, since avoiding
I collision is much easier. `String` and `str` both have many methods, and
L `String` additionally behaves as if it has every method of `str` because of
D deref coercion. The implementing type may also be generic while the
M implementation is still specific in this sense; for example, [`Vec<T>`][vec]
= dereferences to `[T]`, so methods of `T` are not applicable.
L Consider also that deref coercion means that deref traits are a much larger
L part of a type's public API than any other trait as it is implicitly called
H by the compiler. Therefore, it is advisable to consider whether this is
: something you are comfortable supporting as a public API.
L The [`AsRef`] and [`Borrow`][core::borrow::Borrow] traits have very similar
J signatures to `Deref`. It may be desirable to implement either or both of
E these, whether in addition to or rather than deref traits. See their
 # Fallibility
M **This trait's method should never unexpectedly fail**. Deref coercion means
K the compiler will often insert calls to `Deref::deref` implicitly. Failure
H during dereferencing can be extremely confusing when `Deref` is invoked
K implicitly. In the majority of uses it should be infallible, though it may
L be acceptable to panic if the type is misused through programmer error, for
E However, infallibility is not enforced and therefore not guaranteed.
G As such, `unsafe` code should not rely on infallibility in general for
 soundness.

# Custom code within the destructor.
N When a value is no longer needed, Rust will run a "destructor" on that value.
L The most common way that a value is no longer needed is when it goes out of
L scope. Destructors may still run in other circumstances, but we're going to
P focus on scope for the examples here. To learn about some of those other cases,
3 please see [the reference] section on destructors.
F [the reference]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/destructors.html
, This destructor consists of two components:
c - A call to `Drop::drop` for that value, if this special `Drop` trait is implemented for its type.
R - The automatically generated "drop glue" which recursively calls the destructors
#   of all the fields of this value.
E As Rust automatically calls the destructors of all contained fields,
Q you don't have to implement `Drop` in most cases. But there are some cases where
F it is useful, for example for types which directly manage a resource.
V That resource may be memory, it may be a file descriptor, it may be a network socket.
R Once a value of that type is no longer going to be used, it should "clean up" its
F resource by freeing the memory or closing the file or socket. This is
@ the job of a destructor, and therefore the job of `Drop::drop`.
J To see destructors in action, let's take a look at the following program:
 struct HasDrop;
 impl Drop for HasDrop {
'         println!("Dropping HasDrop!");
 struct HasTwoDrops {
     one: HasDrop,
     two: HasDrop,
 impl Drop for HasTwoDrops {
+         println!("Dropping HasTwoDrops!");
9     let _x = HasTwoDrops { one: HasDrop, two: HasDrop };
     println!("Running!");
T Rust will first call `Drop::drop` for `_x` and then for both `_x.one` and `_x.two`,
% meaning that running this will print
	 Running!
 Dropping HasTwoDrops!
 Dropping HasDrop!
q Even if we remove the implementation of `Drop` for `HasTwoDrop`, the destructors of its fields are still called.
 This would result in
 ```test
) ## You cannot call `Drop::drop` yourself
^ Because `Drop::drop` is used to clean up a value, it may be dangerous to use this value after
R the method has been called. As `Drop::drop` does not take ownership of its input,
H Rust prevents misuse by not allowing you to call `Drop::drop` directly.
o In other words, if you tried to explicitly call `Drop::drop` in the above example, you'd get a compiler error.
_ If you'd like to explicitly call the destructor of a value, [`mem::drop`] can be used instead.
 ## Drop order
K Which of our two `HasDrop` drops first, though? For structs, it's the same
K order that they're declared: first `one`, then `two`. If you'd like to try
L this yourself, you can modify `HasDrop` above to contain some data, like an
N integer, and then use it in the `println!` inside of `Drop`. This behavior is

B Unlike for structs, local variables are dropped in reverse order:

# ## `Copy` and `Drop` are exclusive
K You cannot implement both [`Copy`] and `Drop` on the same type. Types that
E are `Copy` get implicitly duplicated by the compiler, making it very
K hard to predict when, and how often destructors will be executed. As such,
% these types cannot have destructors.
 ## Drop check
_ Dropping interacts with the borrow checker in subtle ways: when a type `T` is being implicitly
a dropped as some variable of this type goes out of scope, the borrow checker needs to ensure that
\ calling `T`'s destructor at this moment is safe. In particular, it also needs to be safe to
` recursively drop all the fields of `T`. For example, it is crucial that code like the following
 is being rejected:
 ```compile_fail,E0597
1 struct S<'a>(Cell<Option<&'a S<'a>>>, Box<i32>);
 impl Drop for S<'_> {
(         if let Some(r) = self.0.get() {
7             // Print the contents of the `Box` in `r`.
!             println!("{}", r.1);
0     // Set up two `S` that point to each other.
/     let s1 = S(Cell::new(None), Box::new(42));
4     let s2 = S(Cell::new(Some(&s1)), Box::new(42));
     s1.0.set(Some(&s2));
?     // Now they both get dropped. But whichever is the 2nd one
=     // to be dropped will access the `Box` in the first one,
"     // which is a use-after-free!
L The Nomicon discusses the need for [drop check in more detail][drop check].
\ To reject such code, the "drop check" analysis determines which types and lifetimes need to
T still be live when `T` gets dropped. The exact details of this analysis are not yet
W stably guaranteed and **subject to change**. Currently, the analysis works as follows:
^ - If `T` has no drop glue, then trivially nothing is required to be live. This is the case if
b   neither `T` nor any of its (recursive) fields have a destructor (`impl Drop`). [`PhantomData`],
_   arrays of length 0 and [`ManuallyDrop`] are considered to never have a destructor, no matter
   their field type.
V - If `T` has drop glue, then, for all types `U` that are *owned* by any field of `T`,
a   recursively add the types and lifetimes that need to be live when `U` gets dropped. The set of
;   owned types is determined by recursively traversing `T`:
^   - Recursively descend through `PhantomData`, `Box`, tuples, and arrays (excluding arrays of
     length 0).
]   - Stop at reference and raw pointer types as well as function pointers and function items;
     they do not own anything.
`   - Stop at non-composite types (type parameters that remain generic in the current context and
D     base types such as integers and `bool`); these types are owned.
J   - When hitting an ADT with `impl Drop`, stop there; this type is owned.
`   - When hitting an ADT without `impl Drop`, recursively descend to its fields. (For an `enum`,
*     consider all fields of all variants.)
` - Furthermore, if `T` implements `Drop`, then all generic (lifetime and type) parameters of `T`
   must be live.
^ In the above example, the last clause implies that `'a` must be live when `S<'a>` is dropped,
Z and hence the example is rejected. If we remove the `impl Drop`, the liveness requirement
( disappears and the example is accepted.
\ There exists an unstable way for a type to opt-out of the last clause; this is called "drop
X check eyepatch" or `may_dangle`. For more details on this nightly-only feature, see the

 # Note to Implementors
8 The choice of this type is critical to interconversion.
B Unlike the `Output` type, which will often be a raw generic type,
B this type is typically a newtype of some sort to "color" the type
@ so that it's distinguishable from the residuals of other types.
N This is why `Result<T, E>::Residual` is not `E`, but `Result<Infallible, E>`.
E That way it's distinct from `ControlFlow<E>::Residual`, for example,
M and thus `?` on `ControlFlow` cannot be used in a method returning `Result`.
L If you're making a generic type `Foo<T>` that implements `Try<Output = T>`,
M then typically you can use `Foo<std::convert::Infallible>` as its `Residual`
O type: that type will have a "hole" in the correct place, and will maintain the
M "foo-ness" of the residual so other types need to opt-in to interconversion.

 # `Any` and `TypeId`
L `Any` itself can be used to get a `TypeId`, and has more features when used
L as a trait object. As `&dyn Any` (a borrowed trait object), it has the `is`
O and `downcast_ref` methods, to test if the contained value is of a given type,
N and to get a reference to the inner value as a type. As `&mut dyn Any`, there
J is also the `downcast_mut` method, for getting a mutable reference to the
J inner value. `Box<dyn Any>` adds the `downcast` method, which attempts to
K convert to a `Box<T>`. See the [`Box`] documentation for the full details.
M Note that `&dyn Any` is limited to testing whether a value is of a specified
M concrete type, and cannot be used to test whether a type implements a trait.
 # Smart pointers and `dyn Any`

L especially with types like `Box<dyn Any>` or `Arc<dyn Any>`, is that simply
C calling `.type_id()` on the value will produce the `TypeId` of the
E *container*, not the underlying trait object. This can be avoided by
J converting the smart pointer into a `&dyn Any` instead, which will return
$ the object's `TypeId`. For example:

& # Note on performance and stack usage
I Note that this method is *eager*.  It evaluates `f` all `N` times before
 returning the new array.
H That means that `arr.map(f).map(g)` is, in general, *not* equivalent to
L `array.map(|x| g(f(x)))`, as the former calls `f` 4 times then `g` 4 times,
7 whereas the latter interleaves the calls (`fgfgfgfg`).
N A consequence of this is that it can have fairly-high stack usage, especially
J in debug mode or for long arrays.  The backend may be able to optimize it
G away, but especially for complicated mappings it might not be able to.
I If you're doing a one-step `map` and really want an array as the result,
L then absolutely use this method.  Its implementation uses a bunch of tricks
G to help the optimizer handle it well.  Particularly for simple arrays,
E like `[u8; 3]` or `[f32; 4]`, there's nothing to be concerned about.
L However, if you don't actually need an *array* of the results specifically,
F just to process them, then you likely want [`Iterator::map`] instead.
I For example, rather than doing an array-to-array map of all the elements
? in the array up-front and only iterating after that completes,

# Composable asynchronous iteration.
G If you've found yourself with an asynchronous collection of some kind,
G and needed to perform an operation on the elements of said collection,
O you'll quickly run into 'async iterators'. Async Iterators are heavily used in
M idiomatic asynchronous Rust code, so it's worth becoming familiar with them.
H Before explaining more, let's talk about how this module is structured:
 # Organization
* This module is largely organized by type:
R * [Traits] are the core portion: these traits define what kind of async iterators
M   exist and what you can do with them. The methods of these traits are worth
&   putting some extra study time into.
L * Functions provide some helpful ways to create some basic async iterators.
D * Structs are often the return types of the various methods on this
J   module's traits. You'll usually want to look at the method that creates
L   the `struct`, rather than the `struct` itself. For more detail about why,
E   see '[Implementing Async Iterator](#implementing-async-iterator)'.
 [Traits]: #traits
+ That's it! Let's dig into async iterators.
 # Async Iterators
N The heart and soul of this module is the [`AsyncIterator`] trait. The core of
# [`AsyncIterator`] looks like this:
# # use core::task::{Context, Poll};
 # use core::pin::Pin;
 trait AsyncIterator {
     type Item;
Z     fn poll_next(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Option<Self::Item>>;
Q Unlike `Iterator`, `AsyncIterator` makes a distinction between the [`poll_next`]
U method which is used when implementing an `AsyncIterator`, and a (to-be-implemented)
[ `next` method which is used when consuming an async iterator. Consumers of `AsyncIterator`
H only need to consider `next`, which when called, returns a future which
& yields `Option<AsyncIterator::Item>`.
K The future returned by `next` will yield `Some(Item)` as long as there are
M elements, and once they've all been exhausted, will yield `None` to indicate
J that iteration is finished. If we're waiting on something asynchronous to
P resolve, the future will wait until the async iterator is ready to yield again.
Q Individual async iterators may choose to resume iteration, and so calling `next`
H again may or may not eventually yield `Some(Item)` again at some point.
P [`AsyncIterator`]'s full definition includes a number of other methods as well,
L but they are default methods, built on top of [`poll_next`], and so you get
 them for free.
 [`Poll`]: super::task::Poll
( [`poll_next`]: AsyncIterator::poll_next

R Creating an async iterator of your own involves two steps: creating a `struct` to
R hold the async iterator's state, and then implementing [`AsyncIterator`] for that
 `struct`.

 # Laziness
T Async iterators are *lazy*. This means that just creating an async iterator doesn't
M _do_ a whole lot. Nothing really happens until you call `poll_next`. This is
T sometimes a source of confusion when creating an async iterator solely for its side
@ effects. The compiler will warn us about this kind of behavior:
S warning: unused result that must be used: async iterators do nothing unless polled
1 A trait for dealing with asynchronous iterators.
U This is the main async iterator trait. For more about the concept of async iterators
K generally, please see the [module-level documentation]. In particular, you
; may want to know how to [implement `AsyncIterator`][impl].
) [module-level documentation]: index.html
/ [impl]: index.html#implementing-async-iterator

Stream
1 The type of items yielded by the async iterator.
L Attempts to pull out the next value of this async iterator, registering the
I current task for wakeup if the value is not yet available, and returning
+ `None` if the async iterator is exhausted.
E There are several possible return values, each indicating a distinct
 async iterator state:
K - `Poll::Pending` means that this async iterator's next value is not ready
J   yet. Implementations will ensure that the current task will be notified
$   when the next value may be ready.
J - `Poll::Ready(Some(val))` means that the async iterator has successfully
H   produced a value, `val`, and may produce further values on subsequent
   `poll_next` calls.
H - `Poll::Ready(None)` means that the async iterator has terminated, and
+   `poll_next` should not be invoked again.
[ Once an async iterator has finished (returned `Ready(None)` from `poll_next`), calling its
K `poll_next` method again may panic, block forever, or cause other kinds of
M problems; the `AsyncIterator` trait places no requirements on the effects of
H such a call. However, as the `poll_next` method is not marked `unsafe`,
D Rust's usual rules apply: calls must never cause undefined behavior
G (memory corruption, incorrect use of `unsafe` functions, or the like),
* regardless of the async iterator's state.
B Returns the bounds on the remaining length of the async iterator.
D Specifically, `size_hint()` returns a tuple where the first element
? is the lower bound, and the second element is the upper bound.
T The second half of the tuple that is returned is an <code>[Option]<[usize]></code>.
H A [`None`] here means that either there is no known upper bound, or the
& upper bound is larger than [`usize`].
 # Implementation notes
M It is not enforced that an async iterator implementation yields the declared
O number of elements. A buggy async iterator may yield less than the lower bound
* or more than the upper bound of elements.
I `size_hint()` is primarily intended to be used for optimizations such as
H reserving space for the elements of the async iterator, but must not be
A trusted to e.g., omit bounds checks in unsafe code. An incorrect
A implementation of `size_hint()` should not lead to memory safety
 violations.
C That said, the implementation should provide a correct estimation,
C because otherwise it would be a violation of the trait's protocol.
U The default implementation returns <code>(0, [None])</code> which is correct for any
 async iterator.
H A helper function for internal desugaring -- produces `Ready(Some(t))`,
: which corresponds to the async iterator yielding a value.
A A helper constant for internal desugaring -- produces `Pending`,
@ which corresponds to the async iterator pending on an `.await`.
E A helper constant for internal desugaring -- produces `Ready(None)`,
A which corresponds to the async iterator finishing its iteration.

 Shareable mutable containers.
V Rust memory safety is based on this rule: Given an object `T`, it is only possible to
 have one of the following:
R - Several immutable references (`&T`) to the object (also known as **aliasing**).
Q - One mutable reference (`&mut T`) to the object (also known as **mutability**).
\ This is enforced by the Rust compiler. However, there are situations where this rule is not
[ flexible enough. Sometimes it is required to have multiple references to an object and yet
 mutate it.
\ Shareable mutable containers exist to permit mutability in a controlled manner, even in the
[ presence of aliasing. [`Cell<T>`], [`RefCell<T>`], and [`OnceCell<T>`] allow doing this in
X a single-threaded way
they do not implement [`Sync`]. (If you need to do aliasing and
\ mutation among multiple threads, [`Mutex<T>`], [`RwLock<T>`], [`OnceLock<T>`] or [`atomic`]
1 types are the correct data structures to do so).
] Values of the `Cell<T>`, `RefCell<T>`, and `OnceCell<T>` types may be mutated through shared
\ references (i.e. the common `&T` type), whereas most Rust types can only be mutated through
T unique (`&mut T`) references. We say these cell types provide 'interior mutability'
\ (mutable via `&T`), in contrast with typical Rust types that exhibit 'inherited mutability'
 (mutable only via `&mut T`).
\ Cell types come in four flavors: `Cell<T>`, `RefCell<T>`, `OnceCell<T>`, and `LazyCell<T>`.
E Each provides a different way of providing safe interior mutability.
 ## `Cell<T>`
_ [`Cell<T>`] implements interior mutability by moving values in and out of the cell. That is, a
W `&T` to the inner value can never be obtained, and the value itself cannot be directly
T obtained without replacing it with something else. This type provides the following
	 methods:
Z  - For types that implement [`Copy`], the [`get`](Cell::get) method retrieves the current
%    interior value by duplicating it.
^  - For types that implement [`Default`], the [`take`](Cell::take) method replaces the current
N    interior value with [`Default::default()`] and returns the replaced value.
  - All types have:
^    - [`replace`](Cell::replace): replaces the current interior value and returns the replaced
      value.
Z    - [`into_inner`](Cell::into_inner): this method consumes the `Cell<T>` and returns the
      interior value.
_    - [`set`](Cell::set): this method replaces the interior value, dropping the replaced value.
[ `Cell<T>` is typically used for more simple types where copying or moving values isn't too
^ resource intensive (e.g. numbers), and should usually be preferred over other cell types when
M possible. For larger and non-copy types, `RefCell` provides some advantages.
 ## `RefCell<T>`
a [`RefCell<T>`] uses Rust's lifetimes to implement "dynamic borrowing", a process whereby one can
] claim temporary, exclusive, mutable access to the inner value. Borrows for `RefCell<T>`s are
V tracked at _runtime_, unlike Rust's native reference types which are entirely tracked
 statically, at compile time.
P An immutable reference to a `RefCell`'s inner value (`&T`) can be obtained with
T [`borrow`](`RefCell::borrow`), and a mutable borrow (`&mut T`) can be obtained with
_ [`borrow_mut`](`RefCell::borrow_mut`). When these functions are called, they first verify that
X Rust's borrow rules will be satisfied: any number of immutable borrows are allowed or a
^ single mutable borrow is allowed, but never both. If a borrow is attempted that would violate
$ these rules, the thread will panic.
E The corresponding [`Sync`] version of `RefCell<T>` is [`RwLock<T>`].
 ## `OnceCell<T>`
[ [`OnceCell<T>`] is somewhat of a hybrid of `Cell` and `RefCell` that works for values that
] typically only need to be set once. This means that a reference `&T` can be obtained without
Z moving or copying the inner value (unlike `Cell`) but also without runtime checks (unlike
Z `RefCell`). However, its value can also not be updated once set unless you have a mutable
 reference to the `OnceCell`.
+ `OnceCell` provides the following methods:
@ - [`get`](OnceCell::get): obtain a reference to the inner value
R - [`set`](OnceCell::set): set the inner value if it is unset (returns a `Result`)
\ - [`get_or_init`](OnceCell::get_or_init): return the inner value, initializing it if needed
a - [`get_mut`](OnceCell::get_mut): provide a mutable reference to the inner value, only available
6   if you have a mutable reference to the cell itself.
H The corresponding [`Sync`] version of `OnceCell<T>` is [`OnceLock<T>`].
 ## `LazyCell<T, F>`
[ A common pattern with OnceCell is, for a given OnceCell, to use the same function on every
[ call to [`OnceCell::get_or_init`] with that cell. This is what is offered by [`LazyCell`],
\ which pairs cells of `T` with functions of `F`, and always calls `F` before it yields `&T`.
^ This happens implicitly by simply attempting to dereference the LazyCell to get its contents,
[ so its use is much more transparent with a place which has been initialized by a constant.
a More complicated patterns that don't fit this description can be built on `OnceCell<T>` instead.
Y `LazyCell` works by providing an implementation of `impl Deref` that calls the function,
R so you can just use it by dereference (e.g. `*lazy_cell` or `lazy_cell.deref()`).
N The corresponding [`Sync`] version of `LazyCell<T, F>` is [`LazyLock<T, F>`].
% # When to choose interior mutability
^ The more common inherited mutability, where one must have unique access to mutate a value, is
^ one of the key language elements that enables Rust to reason strongly about pointer aliasing,
Z statically preventing crash bugs. Because of that, inherited mutability is preferred, and
] interior mutability is something of a last resort. Since cell types enable mutation where it
\ would otherwise be disallowed though, there are occasions when interior mutability might be
* appropriate, or even *must* be used, e.g.
9 * Introducing mutability 'inside' of something immutable
9 * Implementation details of logically-immutable methods.
) * Mutating implementations of [`Clone`].

A impossible to mutate data inside of these smart pointers at all.

4 The core primitive for interior mutability in Rust.
a If you have a reference `&T`, then normally in Rust the compiler performs optimizations based on
] the knowledge that `&T` points to immutable data. Mutating that data, for example through an
R alias or by transmuting a `&T` into a `&mut T`, is considered undefined behavior.
T `UnsafeCell<T>` opts-out of the immutability guarantee for `&T`: a shared reference
` `&UnsafeCell<T>` may point to data that is being mutated. This is called "interior mutability".
c All other types that allow internal mutability, such as [`Cell<T>`] and [`RefCell<T>`], internally
% use `UnsafeCell` to wrap their data.
a Note that only the immutability guarantee for shared references is affected by `UnsafeCell`. The
] uniqueness guarantee for mutable references is unaffected. There is *no* legal way to obtain
0 aliasing `&mut`, not even with `UnsafeCell<T>`.
^ `UnsafeCell` does nothing to avoid data races; they are still undefined behavior. If multiple
V threads have access to the same `UnsafeCell`, they must follow the usual rules of the
^ [concurrent memory model]: conflicting non-synchronized accesses must be done via the APIs in
 [`core::sync::atomic`].
[ The `UnsafeCell` API itself is technically very simple: [`.get()`] gives you a raw pointer
` `*mut T` to its contents. It is up to _you_ as the abstraction designer to use that raw pointer
 correctly.
 [`.get()`]: `UnsafeCell::get`
V [concurrent memory model]: ../sync/atomic/index.html#memory-model-for-atomic-accesses
 # Aliasing rules
_ The precise Rust aliasing rules are somewhat in flux, but the main points are not contentious:
` - If you create a safe reference with lifetime `'a` (either a `&T` or `&mut T` reference), then
_   you must not access the data in any way that contradicts that reference for the remainder of
b   `'a`. For example, this means that if you take the `*mut T` from an `UnsafeCell<T>` and cast it
]   to an `&T`, then the data in `T` must remain immutable (modulo any `UnsafeCell` data found
]   within `T`, of course) until that reference's lifetime expires. Similarly, if you create a
a   `&mut T` reference that is released to safe code, then you must not access the data within the
-   `UnsafeCell` until that reference expires.
\ - For both `&T` without `UnsafeCell<_>` and `&mut T`, you must also not deallocate the data
]   until the reference expires. As a special exception, given an `&T`, any part of it that is
_   inside an `UnsafeCell<_>` may be deallocated during the lifetime of the reference, after the
c   last time the reference is used (dereferenced or reborrowed). Since you cannot deallocate a part
d   of what a reference points to, this means the memory an `&T` points to can be deallocated only if
D   *every part of it* (including padding) is inside an `UnsafeCell`.
\ However, whenever a `&UnsafeCell<T>` is constructed or dereferenced, it must still point to
[ live memory and the compiler is allowed to insert spurious reads if it can prove that this
% memory has not yet been deallocated.
T To assist with proper design, the following scenarios are explicitly declared legal
 for single-threaded code:
[ 1. A `&T` reference can be released to safe code and there it can co-exist with other `&T`
'    references, but not with a `&mut T`
^ 2. A `&mut T` reference may be released to safe code provided neither other `&mut T` nor `&T`
7    co-exist with it. A `&mut T` must always be unique.
P Note that whilst mutating the contents of an `&UnsafeCell<T>` (even while other
/ `&UnsafeCell<T>` references alias the cell) is
^ ok (provided you enforce the above invariants some other way), it is still undefined behavior
R to have multiple `&mut UnsafeCell<T>` aliases. That is, `UnsafeCell` is a wrapper
R designed to have a special interaction with _shared_ accesses (_i.e._, through an
X `&UnsafeCell<_>` reference); there is no magic whatsoever when dealing with _exclusive_
Z accesses (_e.g._, through a `&mut UnsafeCell<_>`): neither the cell nor the wrapped value
7 may be aliased for the duration of that `&mut` borrow.
W This is showcased by the [`.get_mut()`] accessor, which is a _safe_ getter that yields
 a `&mut T`.
& [`.get_mut()`]: `UnsafeCell::get_mut`
[ `UnsafeCell<T>` has the same in-memory representation as its inner type `T`. A consequence
U of this guarantee is that it is possible to convert between `T` and `UnsafeCell<T>`.
W Special care has to be taken when converting a nested `T` inside of an `Outer<T>` type
^ to an `Outer<UnsafeCell<T>>` type: this is not sound when the `Outer<T>` type enables [niche]
Y optimizations. For example, the type `Option<NonNull<u8>>` is typically 8 bytes large on
] 64-bit platforms, but the type `Option<UnsafeCell<NonNull<u8>>>` takes up 16 bytes of space.
_ Therefore this is not a valid conversion, despite `NonNull<u8>` and `UnsafeCell<NonNull<u8>>>`
\ having the same memory layout. This is because `UnsafeCell` disables niche optimizations in
_ order to avoid its interior mutability property from spreading from `T` into the `Outer` type,
A thus this can cause distortions in the type size in these cases.
O Note that the only valid way to obtain a `*mut T` pointer to the contents of a
X _shared_ `UnsafeCell<T>` is through [`.get()`]  or [`.raw_get()`]. A `&mut T` reference
R can be obtained by either dereferencing this pointer or by calling [`.get_mut()`]
P on an _exclusive_ `UnsafeCell<T>`. Even though `T` and `UnsafeCell<T>` have the
I same memory layout, the following is not allowed and undefined behavior:

 # Difference from uppercase
J Currently, there are three classes of characters where [`to_uppercase()`]
- and `to_titlecase()` give different results:
 ## Georgian script
P Each letter in the modern Georgian alphabet can be written in one of two forms:
U the typical lowercase-like "mkhedruli" form, and a variant uppercase-like "mtavruli"
V form. However, unlike uppercase in most cased scripts, mtavruli is not typically used
B to start sentences, denote proper nouns, or for any other purpose
[ in running text. It is instead confined to titles and headings, which are written entirely
N in mtavruli. For this reason, [`to_uppercase()`] applied to a Georgian letter
T will return the mtavruli form, but `to_titlecase()` will return the mkhedruli form.

! ## Iota-subscritped Greek vowels
G In ancient Greek, the long vowels alpha (
), eta (
), and omega (
I were sometimes followed by an iota (
), forming a diphthong. Over time,
J the diphthong pronunciation was slowly lost, with the iota becoming mute.
: Eventually, the 
 disappeared from the spelling as well.
E However, there remains a need to represent ancient texts faithfully.
D Modern editions of ancient Greek texts commonly use a reduced-sized

D which continued to affect pronunciation. The exact standard differs
M between different publications. Some render the mute

P vowel (subscript), while others place it to the right of said vowel (adscript).
< The interaction of mute 
 symbols with casing also varies.
L The Unicode Standard, for its default casing rules, chose to make lowercase
P Greek vowels with iota subscipt (e.g. `'
'`) titlecase to the uppercase vowel
O with iota subscript (`'
'`) but uppercase to the uppercase vowel followed by
M full-size uppercase iota (`"
"`). This is just one convention among many
5 in common use, but it is the one Unicode settled on,
% so it is what this method does also.

 # Iterator
I The heart and soul of this module is the [`Iterator`] trait. The core of

 trait Iterator {
.     fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;
B An iterator has a method, [`next`], which when called, returns an
[ <code>[Option]\<Item></code>. Calling [`next`] will return [`Some(Item)`] as long as there
I are elements, and once they've all been exhausted, will return `None` to
H indicate that iteration is finished. Individual iterators may choose to
J resume iteration, and so calling [`next`] again may or may not eventually
S start returning [`Some(Item)`] again at some point (for example, see [`TryIter`]).
K [`Iterator`]'s full definition includes a number of other methods as well,
G but they are default methods, built on top of [`next`], and so you get
L Iterators are also composable, and it's common to chain them together to do
H more complex forms of processing. See the [Adapters](#adapters) section

 # The three forms of iteration
M There are three common methods which can create iterators from a collection:
& * `iter()`, which iterates over `&T`.
. * `iter_mut()`, which iterates over `&mut T`.
* * `into_iter()`, which iterates over `T`.
H Various things in the standard library may implement one or more of the
 three, where appropriate.

 # Adapters
I Functions which take an [`Iterator`] and return another [`Iterator`] are
D often called 'iterator adapters', as they're a form of the 'adapter
 pattern'.
D Common iterator adapters include [`map`], [`take`], and [`filter`].
# For more, see their documentation.
K If an iterator adapter panics, the iterator will be in an unspecified (but
H memory safe) state.  This state is also not guaranteed to stay the same
I across versions of Rust, so you should avoid relying on the exact values
( returned by an iterator which panicked.
 [`map`]: Iterator::map
 [`take`]: Iterator::take
 [`filter`]: Iterator::filter
K Iterators (and iterator [adapters](#adapters)) are *lazy*. This means that
K just creating an iterator doesn't _do_ a whole lot. Nothing really happens
F until you call [`next`]. This is sometimes a source of confusion when
K creating an iterator solely for its side effects. For example, the [`map`]
9 method calls a closure on each element it iterates over:
 # #![allow(unused_must_use)]
 # #![allow(map_unit_fn)]

# v.iter().map(|x| println!("{x}"));
L This will not print any values, as we only created an iterator, rather than
A using it. The compiler will warn us about this kind of behavior:
A warning: unused result that must be used: iterators are lazy and
 do nothing unless consumed
F The idiomatic way to write a [`map`] for its side effects is to use a
, `for` loop or call the [`for_each`] method:
( v.iter().for_each(|x| println!("{x}"));
 // or
 for x in &v {
! [`for_each`]: Iterator::for_each
E Another common way to evaluate an iterator is to use the [`collect`]
$ method to produce a new collection.

* Transforms an iterator into a collection.
B `collect()` takes ownership of an iterator and produces whichever
I collection type you request. The iterator itself carries no knowledge of
H the eventual container; the target collection is chosen entirely by the
F type you ask `collect()` to return. This makes `collect()` one of the
I more powerful methods in the standard library, and it shows up in a wide
 variety of contexts.
C The most basic pattern in which `collect()` is used is to turn one
E collection into another. You take a collection, call [`iter`] on it,
@ do a bunch of transformations, and then `collect()` at the end.
D `collect()` can also create instances of types that are not typical
D collections. For example, a [`String`] can be built from [`char`]s,
E and an iterator of [`Result<T, E>`][`Result`] items can be collected
B into `Result<Collection<T>, E>`. See the examples below for more.
C Because `collect()` is so general, it can cause problems with type
C inference. As such, `collect()` is one of the few times you'll see
A the syntax affectionately known as the 'turbofish': `::<>`. This
G helps the inference algorithm understand specifically which collection
 you're trying to collect into.

k Importantly, `try_collect()` doesn't require that the outer [`Try`] type also implements [`FromIterator`];

/ # When *shouldn't* an adapter be `TrustedLen`?
G If an adapter makes an iterator *shorter* by a given amount, then it's
I usually incorrect for that adapter to implement `TrustedLen`.  The inner
J iterator might return more than `usize::MAX` items, but there's no way to
J know what `k` elements less than that will be, since the `size_hint` from
D the inner iterator has already saturated and lost that information.
I This is why [`Skip<I>`](crate::iter::Skip) isn't `TrustedLen`, even when
 `I` implements `TrustedLen`.
K This trait must only be implemented when the contract is upheld. Consumers
F of this trait must inspect [`Iterator::size_hint()`]
s upper bound.

J has been moved out and the result of the iterator chain could be inserted

h A unicast address has link-local scope if it has the prefix `fe80::/10`, as per [RFC 4291 section 2.4].
Z Note that this encompasses more addresses than those defined in [RFC 4291 section 2.5.6],
] which describes "Link-Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses" as having the following stricter format:
D | 10 bits  |         54 bits         |          64 bits           |
D +----------+-------------------------+----------------------------+
D |1111111010|           0             |       interface ID         |
r So while currently the only addresses with link-local scope an application will encounter are all in `fe80::/64`,
y this might change in the future with the publication of new standards. More addresses in `fe80::/10` could be allocated,
0 and those addresses will have link-local scope.

 Optional values.
? Type [`Option`] represents an optional value: every [`Option`]
: is either [`Some`] and contains a value, or [`None`], and
< does not. [`Option`] types are very common in Rust code, as
 they have a number of uses:
 * Initial values
3 * Return values for functions that are not defined
4   over their entire input range (partial functions)
H * Return value for otherwise reporting simple errors, where [`None`] is
   returned on error
 * Optional struct fields
. * Struct fields that can be loaned or "taken"
 * Optional function arguments
 * Nullable pointers
. * Swapping things out of difficult situations

" # The question mark operator, `?`
\ Similar to the [`Result`] type, when writing code that calls many functions that return the

E operator, [`?`], hides some of the boilerplate of propagating values

+         (Some(x), Some(y)) => Some(x + y),

&     Some(stack.pop()? + stack.pop()?)

[ Ending the expression with [`?`] will result in the [`Some`]'s unwrapped value, unless the
Z result is [`None`], in which case [`None`] is returned early from the enclosing function.

+ early return of [`None`] that it provides.

L Rust guarantees to optimize the following types `T` such that [`Option<T>`]
D has the same size, alignment, and [function call ABI] as `T`. It is
M therefore sound, when `T` is one of these types, to transmute a value `t` of
D type `T` to type `Option<T>` (producing the value `Some(t)`) and to
K transmute a value `Some(t)` of type `Option<T>` to type `T` (producing the
 value `t`).
? In some of these cases, Rust further guarantees the following:
K - `transmute::<_, Option<T>>([0u8; size_of::<T>()])` is sound and produces
   `Option::<T>::None`
R - `transmute::<_, [u8; size_of::<T>()]>(Option::<T>::None)` is sound and produces
   `[0u8; size_of::<T>()]`
1 These cases are identified by the second column:
 | `T`                                                                 | Transmuting between `[0u8; size_of::<T>()]` and `Option::<T>::None` sound? |

- Types that pin data to a location in memory.
Y It is sometimes useful to be able to rely upon a certain value not being able to *move*,
\ in the sense that its address in memory cannot change. This is useful especially when there
Z are one or more [*pointers*][pointer] pointing at that value. The ability to rely on this

- 1. Not be *moved* out of its memory location
? 2. More generally, remain *valid* at that same memory location
Y is called "pinning." We would say that a value which satisfies these guarantees has been
Z "pinned," in that it has been permanently (until the end of its lifespan) attached to its
\ location in memory, as though pinned to a pinboard. Pinning a value is an incredibly useful
[ building block for [`unsafe`] code to be able to reason about whether a raw pointer to the
[ pinned value is still valid. [As we'll see later][drop-guarantee], once a value is pinned,
[ it is necessarily valid at its memory location until the end of its lifespan. This concept
^ of "pinning" is necessary to implement safe interfaces on top of things like self-referential
_ types and intrusive data structures which cannot currently be modeled in fully safe Rust using
- only borrow-checked [references][reference].
` "Pinning" allows us to put a *value* which exists at some location in memory into a state where
` safe code cannot *move* that value to a different location in memory or otherwise invalidate it
G at its current location (unless it implements [`Unpin`], which we will
` [talk about below][self#unpin]). Anything that wants to interact with the pinned value in a way
Z that has the potential to violate these guarantees must promise that it will not actually
] violate them, using the [`unsafe`] keyword to mark that such a promise is upheld by the user
^ and not the compiler. In this way, we can allow other [`unsafe`] code to rely on any pointers
N that point to the pinned value to be valid to dereference while it is pinned.
\ Note that as long as you don't use [`unsafe`], it's impossible to create or misuse a pinned
O value in a way that is unsound. See the documentation of [`Pin<Ptr>`] for more
` information on the practicalities of how to pin a value and how to use that pinned value from a
- user's perspective without using [`unsafe`].
_ The rest of this documentation is intended to be the source of truth for users of [`Pin<Ptr>`]
a that are implementing the [`unsafe`] pieces of an interface that relies on pinning for validity;
E users of [`Pin<Ptr>`] in safe code do not need to read it in detail.

 # What is "*moving*"?
& [what-is-moving]: self#what-is-moving
U When we say a value is *moved*, we mean that the compiler copies, byte-for-byte, the
W value from one location to another. In a purely mechanical sense, this is identical to
] [`Copy`]ing a value from one place in memory to another. In Rust, "move" carries with it the
Z semantics of ownership transfer from one variable to another, which is the key difference
^ between a [`Copy`] and a move. For the purposes of this module's documentation, however, when
` we write *move* in italics, we mean *specifically* that the value has *moved* in the mechanical
1 sense of being located at a new place in memory.
] All values in Rust are trivially *moveable*. This means that the address at which a value is
` located is not necessarily stable in between borrows. The compiler is allowed to *move* a value
P to a new address without running any code to notify that value that its address
] has changed. Although the compiler will not insert memory *moves* where no semantic move has
V occurred, there are many places where a value *may* be moved. For example, when doing
/ assignment or passing a value into a function.
# struct AddrTracker(Option<usize>);

E     // If we haven't checked the addr of self yet, store the current
I     // address. If we have, confirm that the current address is the same
+     // as it was last time, or else panic.
#     fn check_for_move(&mut self) {
7         let current_addr = self as *mut Self as usize;
         match self.0 {
1             None => self.0 = Some(current_addr),
D             Some(prev_addr) => assert_eq!(prev_addr, current_addr),

` Common smart-pointer types such as [`Box<T>`] and [`&mut T`] also allow *moving* the underlying
\ *value* they point at: you can move out of a [`Box<T>`], or you can use [`mem::replace`] to
^ move a `T` out of a [`&mut T`]. Therefore, putting a value (such as `tracker` above) behind a
L pointer isn't enough on its own to ensure that its address does not change.
 # What is "pinning"?
( [what-is-pinning]: self#what-is-pinning
_ We say that a value has been *pinned* when it has been put into a state where it is guaranteed
U to remain *located at the same place in memory* from the time it is pinned until its
 [`drop`] is called.
8 ## Address-sensitive values, AKA "when we need pinning"
S [address-sensitive-values]: self#address-sensitive-values-aka-when-we-need-pinning
I Most values in Rust are entirely okay with being *moved* around at-will.
M Types for which it is *always* the case that *any* value of that type can be
\ *moved* at-will should implement [`Unpin`], which we will discuss more [below][self#unpin].
\ [`Pin`] is specifically targeted at allowing the implementation of *safe interfaces* around
] types which have some state during which they become "address-sensitive." A value in such an
] "address-sensitive" state is *not* okay with being *moved* around at-will. Such a value must
\ stay *un-moved* and valid during the address-sensitive portion of its lifespan because some
a interface is relying on those invariants to be true in order for its implementation to be sound.
\ As a motivating example of a type which may become address-sensitive, consider a type which
` contains a pointer to another piece of its own data, *i.e.* a "self-referential" type. In order
_ for such a type to be implemented soundly, the pointer which points into `self`'s data must be
[ proven valid whenever it is accessed. But if that value is *moved*, the pointer will still
^ point to the old address where the value was located and not into the new location of `self`,
[ thus becoming invalid. A key example of such self-referential types are the state machines
C generated by the compiler to implement [`Future`] for `async fn`s.
M Such types that have an *address-sensitive* state usually follow a lifecycle
 that looks something like so:
8 1. A value is created which can be freely moved around.
[     * e.g. calling an async function which returns a state machine implementing [`Future`]
K 2. An operation causes the value to depend on its own address not changing
J     * e.g. calling [`poll`] for the first time on the produced [`Future`]
] 3. Further pieces of the safe interface of the type use internal [`unsafe`] operations which
2    assume that the address of the value is stable
(     * e.g. subsequent calls to [`poll`]
^ 4. Before the value is invalidated (e.g. deallocated), it is *dropped*, giving it a chance to
S    notify anything with pointers to itself that those pointers will be invalidated
:     * e.g. [`drop`]ping the [`Future`] [^pin-drop-future]
Y There are two possible ways to ensure the invariants required for 2. and 3. above (which
Y apply to any address-sensitive type, not just self-referential types) do not get broken.
\ 1. Have the value detect when it is moved and update all the pointers that point to itself.
[ 2. Guarantee that the address of the value does not change (and that memory is not re-used
Z    for anything else) during the time that the pointers to it are expected to be valid to
    dereference.
^ Since, as we discussed, Rust can move values without notifying them that they have moved, the
 first option is ruled out.
X In order to implement the second option, we must in some way enforce its key invariant,
Z *i.e.* prevent the value from being *moved* or otherwise invalidated (you may notice this
^ sounds an awful lot like the definition of *pinning* a value). There are a few ways one might
+ be able to enforce this invariant in Rust:
[ 1. Offer a wholly `unsafe` API to interact with the object, thus requiring every caller to
#    uphold the invariant themselves
Y 2. Store the value that must not be moved behind a carefully managed pointer internal to
    the object
\ 3. Leverage the type system to encode and enforce this invariant by presenting a restricted
L    API surface to interact with *any* object that requires these invariants
[ The first option is quite obviously undesirable, as the [`unsafe`]ty of the interface will
A become viral throughout all code that interacts with the object.
X The second option is a viable solution to the problem for some use cases, in particular
[ for self-referential types. Under this model, any type that has an address sensitive state
Z would ultimately store its data in something like a [`Box<T>`], carefully manage internal
S access to that data to ensure no *moves* or other invalidation occurs, and finally
! provide a safe interface on top.
] There are a couple of linked disadvantages to using this model. The most significant is that
@ each individual object must assume it is *on its own* to ensure
Y that its data does not become *moved* or otherwise invalidated. Since there is no shared
\ contract between values of different types, an object cannot assume that others interacting
W with it will properly respect the invariants around interacting with its data and must
^ therefore protect it from everyone. Because of this, *composition* of address-sensitive types
\ requires at least a level of pointer indirection each time a new object is added to the mix
' (and, practically, a heap allocation).
` Although there were other reasons as well, this issue of expensive composition is the key thing
Q that drove Rust towards adopting a different model. It is particularly a problem
^ when one considers, for example, the implications of composing together the [`Future`]s which
[ will eventually make up an asynchronous task (including address-sensitive `async fn` state
] machines). It is plausible that there could be many layers of [`Future`]s composed together,
[ including multiple layers of `async fn`s handling different parts of a task. It was deemed
] unacceptable to force indirection and allocation for each layer of composition in this case.
X [`Pin<Ptr>`] is an implementation of the third option. It allows us to solve the issues
X discussed with the second option by building a *shared contractual language* around the
 guarantees of "pinning" data.
Z [^pin-drop-future]: Futures themselves do not ever need to notify other bits of code that
\ they are being dropped, however data structures like stack-based intrusive linked lists do.
$ ## Using [`Pin<Ptr>`] to pin values
U In order to pin a value, we wrap a *pointer to that value* (of some type `Ptr`) in a
] [`Pin<Ptr>`]. [`Pin<Ptr>`] can wrap any pointer type, forming a promise that the **pointee**
@ will not be *moved* or [otherwise invalidated][subtle-details].
` We call such a [`Pin`]-wrapped pointer a **pinning pointer,** (or pinning reference, or pinning
\ `Box`, etc.) because its existence is the thing that is conceptually pinning the underlying
Z pointee in place: it is the metaphorical "pin" securing the data in place on the pinboard
 (in memory).
[ Notice that the thing wrapped by [`Pin`] is not the value which we want to pin itself, but
\ rather a pointer to that value! A [`Pin<Ptr>`] does not pin the `Ptr`; instead, it pins the
 pointer's ***pointee** value*.
" ### Pinning as a library contract
Y Pinning does not require nor make use of any compiler "magic"[^noalias], only a specific
F contract between the [`unsafe`] parts of a library API and its users.
[ It is important to stress this point as a user of the [`unsafe`] parts of the [`Pin`] API.
Y Practically, this means that performing the mechanics of "pinning" a value by creating a
W [`Pin<Ptr>`] to it *does not* actually change the way the compiler behaves towards the
[ inner value! It is possible to use incorrect [`unsafe`] code to create a [`Pin<Ptr>`] to a
^ value which does not actually satisfy the invariants that a pinned value must satisfy, and in
` this way lead to undefined behavior even in (from that point) fully safe code. Similarly, using
L [`unsafe`], one may get access to a bare [`&mut T`] from a [`Pin<Ptr>`] and
T use that to invalidly *move* the pinned value out. It is the job of the user of the
Q [`unsafe`] parts of the [`Pin`] API to ensure these invariants are not violated.
Z This differs from e.g. [`UnsafeCell`] which changes the semantics of a program's compiled
^ output. A [`Pin<Ptr>`] is a handle to a value which we have promised we will not move out of,
\ but Rust still considers all values themselves to be fundamentally moveable through, *e.g.*
  assignment or [`mem::replace`].
^ [^noalias]: There is a bit of nuance here that is still being decided about what the aliasing
D semantics of `Pin<&mut T>` should be, but this is true as of today.
- ### How [`Pin`] prevents misuse in safe code
_ In order to accomplish the goal of pinning the pointee value, [`Pin<Ptr>`] restricts access to
[ the wrapped `Ptr` type in safe code. Specifically, [`Pin`] disallows the ability to access
` the wrapped pointer in ways that would allow the user to *move* the underlying pointee value or
Y otherwise re-use that memory for something else without using [`unsafe`]. For example, a
_ [`Pin<&mut T>`] makes it impossible to obtain the wrapped <code>[&mut] T</code> safely because
^ through that <code>[&mut] T</code> it would be possible to *move* the underlying value out of
( the pointer with [`mem::replace`], etc.
\ As discussed above, this promise must be upheld manually by [`unsafe`] code which interacts
X with the [`Pin<Ptr>`] so that other [`unsafe`] code can rely on the pointee value being
` *un-moved* and valid. Interfaces that operate on values which are in an address-sensitive state
Y accept an argument like <code>[Pin]<[&mut] T></code> or <code>[Pin]<[Box]\<T>></code> to
& indicate this contract to the caller.
] [As discussed below][drop-guarantee], opting in to using pinning guarantees in the interface
\ of an address-sensitive type has consequences for the implementation of some safe traits on
 that type as well.
2 ## Interaction between [`Deref`] and [`Pin<Ptr>`]
T Since [`Pin<Ptr>`] can wrap any pointer type, it uses [`Deref`] and [`DerefMut`] in
] order to identify the type of the pinned pointee data and provide (restricted) access to it.
Z A [`Pin<Ptr>`] where [`Ptr: Deref`][Deref] is a "`Ptr`-style pinning pointer" to a pinned
b [`Ptr::Target`][Target] 
 so, a <code>[Pin]<[Box]\<T>></code> is an owned, pinning pointer to a
\ pinned `T`, and a <code>[Pin]<[Rc]\<T>></code> is a reference-counted, pinning pointer to a
 pinned `T`.
] [`Pin<Ptr>`] also uses the [`<Ptr as Deref>::Target`][Target] type information to modify the
W interface it is allowed to provide for interacting with that data (for example, when a
E pinning pointer points at pinned data which implements [`Unpin`], as
  [discussed below][self#unpin]).
[ [`Pin<Ptr>`] requires that implementations of [`Deref`] and [`DerefMut`] on `Ptr` return a
_ pointer to the pinned data directly and do not *move* out of the `self` parameter during their
] implementation of [`DerefMut::deref_mut`]. It is unsound for [`unsafe`] code to wrap pointer
^ types with such "malicious" implementations of [`Deref`]; see [`Pin<Ptr>::new_unchecked`] for
 ## Fixing `AddrTracker`
\ The guarantee of a stable address is necessary to make our `AddrTracker` example work. When
^ `check_for_move` sees a <code>[Pin]<&mut AddrTracker></code>, it can safely assume that value
\ will exist at that same address until said value goes out of scope, and thus multiple calls

N     // remove auto-implemented `Unpin` bound to mark this type as having some
K     // address-sensitive state. This is essential for our expected pinning

 ## [`Unpin`]
N The vast majority of Rust types have no address-sensitive states. These types
M implement the [`Unpin`] auto-trait, which cancels the restrictive effects of
L [`Pin`] when the *pointee* type `T` is [`Unpin`]. When [`T: Unpin`][Unpin],
\ <code>[Pin]<[Box]\<T>></code> functions identically to a non-pinning [`Box<T>`]; similarly,
U <code>[Pin]<[&mut] T></code> would impose no additional restrictions above a regular
 [`&mut T`].
[ The idea of this trait is to alleviate the reduced ergonomics of APIs that require the use
\ of [`Pin`] for soundness for some types, but which also want to be used by other types that
_ don't care about pinning. The prime example of such an API is [`Future::poll`]. There are many
Z [`Future`] types that don't care about pinning. These futures can implement [`Unpin`] and
[ therefore get around the pinning related restrictions in the API, while still allowing the
L subset of [`Future`]s which *do* require pinning to be implemented soundly.
Z Note that the interaction between a [`Pin<Ptr>`] and [`Unpin`] is through the type of the
U **pointee** value, [`<Ptr as Deref>::Target`][Target]. Whether the `Ptr` type itself
a implements [`Unpin`] does not affect the behavior of a [`Pin<Ptr>`]. For example, whether or not
] [`Box`] is [`Unpin`] has no effect on the behavior of <code>[Pin]<[Box]\<T>></code>, because
[ `T` is the type of the pointee value, not [`Box`]. So, whether `T` implements [`Unpin`] is
N the thing that will affect the behavior of the <code>[Pin]<[Box]\<T>></code>.
] Builtin types that are [`Unpin`] include all of the primitive types, like [`bool`], [`i32`],
] and [`f32`], references (<code>[&]T</code> and <code>[&mut] T</code>), etc., as well as many
G core and standard library types like [`Box<T>`], [`String`], and more.
^ These types are marked [`Unpin`] because they do not have an address-sensitive state like the
` ones we discussed above. If they did have such a state, those parts of their interface would be
Q unsound without being expressed through pinning, and they would then need to not
 implement [`Unpin`].
^ The compiler is free to take the conservative stance of marking types as [`Unpin`] so long as
W all of the types that compose its fields are also [`Unpin`]. This is because if a type
S implements [`Unpin`], then it is unsound for that type's implementation to rely on
` pinning-related guarantees for soundness, *even* when viewed through a "pinning" pointer! It is
Z the responsibility of the implementor of a type that relies upon pinning for soundness to
Y ensure that type is *not* marked as [`Unpin`] by adding [`PhantomPinned`] field. This is
] exactly what we did with our `AddrTracker` example above. Without doing this, you *must not*
: rely on pinning-related guarantees to apply to your type!
[ If you really need to pin a value of a foreign or built-in type that implements [`Unpin`],
_ you'll need to create your own wrapper type around the [`Unpin`] type you want to pin and then
. opt-out of [`Unpin`] using [`PhantomPinned`].
Z Exposing access to the inner field which you want to remain pinned must then be carefully
G considered as well! Remember, exposing a method that gives access to a
^ <code>[Pin]<[&mut] InnerT></code> where <code>InnerT: [Unpin]</code> would allow safe code to
[ trivially move the inner value out of that pinning pointer, which is precisely what you're
[ seeking to prevent! Exposing a field of a pinned value through a pinning pointer is called
^ "projecting" a pin, and the more general case of deciding in which cases a pin should be able
^ to be projected or not is called "structural pinning." We will go into more detail about this
 [below][structural-pinning].
