$ ## An intrusive, doubly-linked list
0 [linked-list]: #an-intrusive-doubly-linked-list
[ In an intrusive doubly-linked list, the collection itself does not own the memory in which
_ each of its elements is stored. Instead, each client is free to allocate space for elements it
^ adds to the list in whichever manner it likes, including on the stack! Elements can be stored
\ in a stack frame shorter-lived than the collection, provided they are removed from the list
% before that frame goes out of scope.
` To make such an intrusive data structure work, every element stores pointers to its predecessor
_ and successor within its own data, rather than having the list structure itself managing those
W pointers. It is in this sense that the structure is "intrusive": the details of how an
^ element is stored within the larger structure "intrudes" on the implementation of the element
 type itself!
W The full implementation details of such a data structure are outside the scope of this
B documentation, but we will discuss how [`Pin`] can help to do so.
^ Using such an intrusive pattern, elements may only be added when they are pinned. If we think
W about the consequences of adding non-pinned values to such a list, this becomes clear:
^ *Moving* or otherwise invalidating an element's data would invalidate the pointers back to it
\ which are stored in the elements ahead and behind it. Thus, in order to soundly dereference
Z the pointers stored to the next and previous elements, we must satisfy the guarantee that
Q nothing has invalidated those pointers (which point to data that we do not own).
X Moreover, the [`Drop`][Drop] implementation of each element must in some way notify its
^ predecessor and successor elements that it should be removed from the list before it is fully
M destroyed, otherwise the pointers back to it would again become invalidated.
[ Crucially, this means we have to be able to rely on [`drop`] always being called before an
\ element is invalidated. If an element could be deallocated or otherwise invalidated without
N calling [`drop`], the pointers to it stored in its neighboring elements would
6 become invalid, which would break the data structure.
R Therefore, pinning data also comes with [the "`Drop` guarantee"][drop-guarantee].
* # Subtle details and the `Drop` guarantee
= [subtle-details]: self#subtle-details-and-the-drop-guarantee
= [drop-guarantee]: self#subtle-details-and-the-drop-guarantee
U The purpose of pinning is not *just* to prevent a value from being *moved*, but more
^ generally to be able to rely on the pinned value *remaining valid **at a specific place*** in
 memory.
^ To do so, pinning a value adds an *additional* invariant that must be upheld in order for use
^ of the pinned data to be valid, on top of the ones that must be upheld for a non-pinned value
 of the same type to be valid:
Z From the moment a value is pinned by constructing a [`Pin`]ning pointer to it, that value
Y must *remain, **valid***, at that same address in memory, *until its [`drop`] handler is
	 called.*
[ There is some subtlety to this which we have not yet talked about in detail. The invariant
! described above means that, yes,
= 1. The value must not be moved out of its location in memory
 but it also implies that,
^ 2. The memory location that stores the value must not get invalidated or otherwise repurposed
P    during the lifespan of the pinned value until its [`drop`] returns or panics
[ This point is subtle but required for intrusive data structures to be implemented soundly.
 ## `Drop` guarantee
\ There needs to be a way for a pinned value to notify any code that is relying on its pinned
X status that it is about to be destroyed. In this way, the dependent code can remove the
Z pinned value's address from its data structures or otherwise change its behavior with the
^ knowledge that it can no longer rely on that value existing at the location it was pinned to.
a Thus, in any situation where we may want to overwrite a pinned value, that value's [`drop`] must
` be called beforehand (unless the pinned value implements [`Unpin`], in which case we can ignore
( all of [`Pin`]'s guarantees, as usual).
^ The most common storage-reuse situations occur when a value on the stack is destroyed as part
] of a function return and when heap storage is freed. In both cases, [`drop`] gets run for us
Y by Rust when using standard safe code. However, for manual heap allocations or otherwise
_ custom-allocated storage, [`unsafe`] code must make sure to call [`ptr::drop_in_place`] before
( deallocating and re-using said storage.
\ In addition, storage "re-use"/invalidation can happen even if no storage is (de-)allocated.
_ For example, if we had an [`Option`] which contained a `Some(v)` where `v` is pinned, then `v`
7 would be invalidated by setting that option to `None`.
Y Similarly, if a [`Vec`] was used to store pinned values and [`Vec::set_len`] was used to
_ manually "kill" some elements of a vector, all of the items "killed" would become invalidated,
@ which would be *undefined behavior* if those items were pinned.
_ Both of these cases are somewhat contrived, but it is crucial to remember that [`Pin`]ned data
[ *must* be [`drop`]ped before it is invalidated; not just to prevent memory leaks, but as a
R matter of soundness. As a corollary, the following code can *never* be made safe:
 # use std::mem::ManuallyDrop;
 # use std::pin::Pin;
 # struct Type;
C // Pin something inside a `ManuallyDrop`. This is fine on its own.
O let mut pin: Pin<Box<ManuallyDrop<Type>>> = Box::pin(ManuallyDrop::new(Type));
F // However, creating a pinning mutable reference to the type *inside*
 // the `ManuallyDrop` is not!
% let inner: Pin<&mut Type> = unsafe {
7     Pin::map_unchecked_mut(pin.as_mut(), |x| &mut **x)
[ Because [`mem::ManuallyDrop`] inhibits the destructor of `Type`, it won't get run when the
_ <code>[Box]<[ManuallyDrop]\<Type>></code> is dropped, thus violating the drop guarantee of the
" <code>[Pin]<[&mut] Type>></code>.
a Of course, *leaking* memory in such a way that its underlying storage will never get invalidated
a or re-used is still fine: [`mem::forget`]ing a [`Box<T>`] prevents its storage from ever getting
7 re-used, so the [`drop`] guarantee is still satisfied.
* # Implementing an address-sensitive type.
T This section goes into detail on important considerations for implementing your own
Y address-sensitive types, which are different from merely using [`Pin<Ptr>`] in a generic
 way.
A ## Implementing [`Drop`] for types with address-sensitive states
L [drop-impl]: self#implementing-drop-for-types-with-address-sensitive-states
\ The [`drop`] function takes [`&mut self`], but this is called *even if that `self` has been
r pinned*! Implementing [`Drop`] for a type with address-sensitive states requires some care, because if `self` was
Z indeed in an address-sensitive state before [`drop`] was called, it is as if the compiler
1 automatically called [`Pin::get_unchecked_mut`].
Y This can never cause a problem in purely safe code because creating a pinning pointer to
c a type which has address-sensitive states (and thus does not implement `Unpin`) requires `unsafe`,
Z but it is important to note that choosing to take advantage of pinning-related guarantees
X to justify validity in the implementation of your type has consequences for that type's
Z [`Drop`][Drop] implementation as well: if an element of your type could have been pinned,
Z you must treat [`Drop`][Drop] as implicitly taking <code>self: [Pin]<[&mut] Self></code>.
* You should implement [`Drop`] as follows:
 impl Drop for Type {
L         // `new_unchecked` is okay because we know this value is never used
&         // again after being dropped.
8         inner_drop(unsafe { Pin::new_unchecked(self)});
.         fn inner_drop(this: Pin<&mut Type>) {
+             // Actual drop code goes here.
[ The function `inner_drop` has the signature that [`drop`] *should* have in this situation.
\ This makes sure that you do not accidentally use `self`/`this` in a way that is in conflict
 with pinning's invariants.
W Moreover, if your type is [`#[repr(packed)]`][packed], the compiler will automatically
= move fields around to be able to drop them. It might even do
Y that for fields that happen to be sufficiently aligned. As a consequence, you cannot use
1 pinning with a [`#[repr(packed)]`][packed] type.
W ### Implementing [`Drop`] for pointer types which will be used as [`Pin`]ning pointers
] It should further be noted that creating a pinning pointer of some type `Ptr` *also* carries
H with it implications on the way that `Ptr` type must implement [`Drop`]
^ (as well as [`Deref`] and [`DerefMut`])! When implementing a pointer type that may be used as
\ a pinning pointer, you must also take the same care described above not to *move* out of or
M otherwise invalidate the pointee during [`Drop`], [`Deref`], or [`DerefMut`]
 implementations.
 ## "Assigning" pinned data
_ Although in general it is not valid to swap data or assign through a [`Pin<Ptr>`] for the same
[ reason that reusing a pinned object's memory is invalid, it is possible to do validly when
W implemented with special care for the needs of the exact data structure which is being
] modified. For example, the assigning function must know how to update all uses of the pinned
T address (and any other invariants necessary to satisfy validity for that type). For
W [`Unmovable`] (from the example above), we could write an assignment function like so:
" # use std::marker::PhantomPinned;

;     fn assign(self: Pin<&mut Self>, src: Pin<&mut Self>) {

?             let unpinned_src = Pin::into_inner_unchecked(src);

b Note that it _is_ possible to assign generically through a [`Pin<Ptr>`] by way of [`Pin::set()`].
] This does not violate any guarantees, since it will run [`drop`] on the pointee value before

& ## Projections and Structural Pinning
> [structural-pinning]: self#projections-and-structural-pinning
Y With ordinary structs, it is natural that we want to add *projection* methods that allow
V borrowing one or more of the inner fields of a struct when the caller has access to a
 borrow of the whole struct:
 # struct Field;
 struct Struct {
     field: Field,
 impl Struct {
:     fn field(&mut self) -> &mut Field { &mut self.field }
X When working with address-sensitive types, it's not obvious what the signature of these
_ functions should be. If `field` takes <code>self: [Pin]<[&mut Struct][&mut]></code>, should it
\ return [`&mut Field`] or <code>[Pin]<[`&mut Field`]></code>? This question also arises with
Z `enum`s and wrapper types like [`Vec<T>`], [`Box<T>`], and [`RefCell<T>`]. (This question
] applies just as well to shared references, but we'll examine the more common case of mutable
 references for illustration)
Z It turns out that it's up to the author of `Struct` to decide which type the "projection"
Y should produce. The choice must be *consistent* though: if a pin is projected to a field
Y in one place, then it should very likely not be exposed elsewhere without projecting the
 pin.
T As the author of a data structure, you get to decide for each field whether pinning
X "propagates" to this field or not. Pinning that propagates is also called "structural",
. because it follows the structure of the type.
a This choice depends on what guarantees you need from the field for your [`unsafe`] code to work.
Y If the field is itself address-sensitive, or participates in the parent struct's address
5 sensitivity, it will need to be structurally pinned.
[ A useful test is if [`unsafe`] code that consumes <code>[Pin]\<[&mut Struct][&mut]></code>
_ also needs to take note of the address of the field itself, it may be evidence that that field
I is structurally pinned. Unfortunately, there are no hard-and-fast rules.
; ### Choosing pinning *not to be* structural for `field`...
N While counter-intuitive, it's often the easier choice: if you do not expose a
Q <code>[Pin]<[&mut] Field></code>, you do not need to be careful about other code
R moving out of that field, you just have to ensure that you never create a pinning
[ reference to that field. This does of course also mean that if you decide a field does not
^ have structural pinning, you must not write [`unsafe`] code that assumes (invalidly) that the
  field *is* structurally pinned!
J Fields without structural pinning may have a projection method that turns
7 <code>[Pin]<[&mut] Struct></code> into [`&mut Field`]:
 # type Field = i32;
! # struct Struct { field: Field }
3     fn field(self: Pin<&mut Self>) -> &mut Field {
X         // This is okay because `field` is never considered pinned, therefore we do not
Z         // need to uphold any pinning guarantees for this field in particular. Of course,
V         // we must not elsewhere assume this field *is* pinned if we choose to expose
         // such a method!
7         unsafe { &mut self.get_unchecked_mut().field }
] You may also in this situation <code>impl [Unpin] for Struct {}</code> *even if* the type of
_ `field` is not [`Unpin`]. Since we have explicitly chosen not to care about pinning guarantees
X for `field`, the way `field`'s type interacts with pinning is no longer relevant in the
  context of its use in `Struct`.
7 ### Choosing pinning *to be* structural for `field`...
H The other option is to decide that pinning is "structural" for `field`,
; meaning that if the struct is pinned then so is the field.
Y This allows writing a projection that creates a <code>[Pin]<[`&mut Field`]></code>, thus
% witnessing that the field is pinned:
8     fn field(self: Pin<&mut Self>) -> Pin<&mut Field> {
B         // This is okay because `field` is pinned when `self` is.
<         unsafe { self.map_unchecked_mut(|s| &mut s.field) }
8 Structural pinning comes with a few extra requirements:
I 1.  *Structural [`Unpin`].* A struct can be [`Unpin`] only if all of its
R     structurally-pinned fields are, too. This is [`Unpin`]'s behavior by default.
X     However, as a library author, it is your responsibility not to write something like
Z     <code>impl\<T> [Unpin] for Struct\<T> {}</code> and then offer a method that provides
[     structural pinning to an inner field of `T`, which may not be [`Unpin`]! (Adding *any*
_     projection operation requires unsafe code, so the fact that [`Unpin`] is a safe trait does
U     not break the principle that you only have to worry about any of this if you use
     [`unsafe`])
J 2.  *Pinned Destruction.* As discussed [above][drop-impl], [`drop`] takes
P     [`&mut self`], but the struct (and hence its fields) might have been pinned
B     before. The destructor must be written as if its argument was
7     <code>self: [Pin]\<[`&mut Self`]></code>, instead.
L     As a consequence, the struct *must not* be [`#[repr(packed)]`][packed].
< 3.  *Structural Notice of Destruction.* You must uphold the
`     [`Drop` guarantee][drop-guarantee]: once your struct is pinned, the struct's storage cannot
U     be re-used without calling the structurally-pinned fields' destructors, as well.
[     This can be tricky, as witnessed by [`VecDeque<T>`]: the destructor of [`VecDeque<T>`]
^     can fail to call [`drop`] on all elements if one of the destructors panics. This violates
^     the [`Drop` guarantee][drop-guarantee], because it can lead to elements being deallocated
+     without their destructor being called.
Y     [`VecDeque<T>`] has no pinning projections, so its destructor is sound. If it wanted
^     to provide such structural pinning, its destructor would need to abort the process if any
!     of the destructors panicked.
Y 4.  You must not offer any other operations that could lead to data being *moved* out of
[     the structural fields when your type is pinned. For example, if the struct contains an
Q     [`Option<T>`] and there is a [`take`][Option::take]-like operation with type
F     <code>fn([Pin]<[&mut Struct\<T>][&mut]>) -> [`Option<T>`]</code>,
X     then that operation can be used to move a `T` out of a pinned `Struct<T>` 
 which
H     means pinning cannot be structural for the field holding this data.
D     For a more complex example of moving data out of a pinned type,
+     imagine if [`RefCell<T>`] had a method
R     <code>fn get_pin_mut(self: [Pin]<[`&mut Self`]>) -> [Pin]<[`&mut T`]></code>.
$     Then we could do the following:
     ```compile_fail
;     fn exploit_ref_cell<T>(mut rc: Pin<&mut RefCell<T>>) {
1         // Here we get pinned access to the `T`.
8         let _: Pin<&mut T> = rc.as_mut().get_pin_mut();
7         // And here we have `&mut T` to the same data.
;         let shared: &RefCell<T> = rc.into_ref().get_ref();
.         let mut borrow = shared.borrow_mut();
$         let content = &mut *borrow;
     ```
G     This is catastrophic: it means we can first pin the content of the
R     [`RefCell<T>`] (using <code>[RefCell]::get_pin_mut</code>) and then move that
6     content using the mutable reference we got later.
  ### Structural Pinning examples
P For a type like [`Vec<T>`], both possibilities (structural pinning or not) make
O sense. A [`Vec<T>`] with structural pinning could have `get_pin`/`get_pin_mut`
U methods to get pinning references to elements. However, it could *not* allow calling
S [`pop`][Vec::pop] on a pinned [`Vec<T>`] because that would move the (structurally
_ pinned) contents! Nor could it allow [`push`][Vec::push], which might reallocate and thus also
 move the contents.
. A [`Vec<T>`] without structural pinning could
T <code>impl\<T> [Unpin] for [`Vec<T>`]</code>, because the contents are never pinned
< and the [`Vec<T>`] itself is fine with being moved as well.
? At that point pinning just has no effect on the vector at all.
Q In the standard library, pointer types generally do not have structural pinning,
] and thus they do not offer pinning projections. This is why <code>[`Box<T>`]: [Unpin]</code>
S holds for all `T`. It makes sense to do this for pointer types, because moving the
H [`Box<T>`] does not actually move the `T`: the [`Box<T>`] can be freely
a movable (aka [`Unpin`]) even if the `T` is not. In fact, even <code>[Pin]<[`Box<T>`]></code> and
U <code>[Pin]<[`&mut T`]></code> are always [`Unpin`] themselves, for the same reason:
] their contents (the `T`) are pinned, but the pointers themselves can be moved without moving
I the pinned data. For both [`Box<T>`] and <code>[Pin]<[`Box<T>`]></code>,
E whether the content is pinned is entirely independent of whether the
8 pointer is pinned, meaning pinning is *not* structural.
T When implementing a [`Future`] combinator, you will usually need structural pinning
[ for the nested futures, as you need to get pinning ([`Pin`]-wrapped) references to them to

% A module for working with processes.
I Most process-related functionality requires std, but [`abort_immediate`]
 is available on all targets.
- Terminates the process in a violent fashion.
J The function will never return and will immediately terminate the current
D process in a platform specific "abnormal" manner. As a consequence,
@ no destructors on the current stack or any other thread's stack
I will be run, Rust IO buffers (eg, from `BufWriter`) will not be flushed,
) and C stdio buffers will not be flushed.
J Unlike [`abort`](../../std/process/fn.abort.html), `abort_immediate` does
G not attempt to match C `abort()` or otherwise perform a "clean" abort.
K Instead, it emits code that will crash the process with as little overhead
K as possible, such as a "halt and catch fire" style instruction. You should
I generally prefer using `abort` instead except where the absolute minimum
 overhead is required.
 # Platform-specific behavior
K `abort_immediate` lowers to a trap instruction on *most* architectures; on
L some architectures it simply lowers to call the unmangled `abort` function.
9 The exact behavior is architecture and system dependent.
D On bare-metal (no OS) systems the trap instruction usually causes a
G *hardware* exception to be raised in a *synchronous* fashion; hardware
D exceptions have nothing to do with C++ exceptions and are closer in
 semantics to POSIX signals.
D On hosted applications (applications running under an OS), the trap
J instruction *usually* terminates the whole process with an exit code that
H corresponds to `SIGILL` or equivalent, *unless* this signal is handled.
K Other signals such as `SIGABRT`, `SIGTRAP`, `SIGSEGV`, and `SIGBUS` may be
J produced instead, depending on specifics. This is not an exhaustive list.

' Error handling with the `Result` type.
J [`Result<T, E>`][`Result`] is the type used for returning and propagating
A errors. It is an enum with the variants, [`Ok(T)`], representing
C success and containing a value, and [`Err(E)`], representing error
 and containing an error value.
 enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),
    Err(E),

@ A common problem with using return values to indicate errors is
C that it is easy to ignore the return value, thus failing to handle
E the error. [`Result`] is annotated with the `#[must_use]` attribute,
? which will cause the compiler to issue a warning when a Result
? value is ignored. This makes [`Result`] especially useful with
A functions that may encounter errors but don't otherwise return a

> is just a synonym for <code>[Result]<T, [io::Error]></code>.*

A You might instead, if you don't want to handle the error, simply

D In some cases, [`Result<T, E>`] comes with size, alignment, and ABI
K guarantees. Specifically, one of either the `T` or `E` type must be a type
L that qualifies for the `Option` [representation guarantees][opt-rep] (let's
D call that type `I`), and the *other* type is a zero-sized type with
 alignment 1 (a "1-ZST").
K If that is the case, then `Result<T, E>` has the same size, alignment, and
K [function call ABI] as `I` (and therefore, as `Option<I>`). If `I` is `T`,
C it is therefore sound to transmute a value `t` of type `I` to type
F `Result<T, E>` (producing the value `Ok(t)`) and to transmute a value
M `Ok(t)` of type `Result<T, E>` to type `I` (producing the value `t`). If `I`
6 is `E`, the same applies with `Ok` replaced by `Err`.
D For example, `NonZeroI32` qualifies for the `Option` representation
K guarantees and `()` is a zero-sized type with alignment 1. This means that
I both `Result<NonZeroI32, ()>` and `Result<(), NonZeroI32>` have the same
I size, alignment, and ABI as `NonZeroI32` (and `Option<NonZeroI32>`). The
; only difference between these is in the implied semantics:
< * `Option<NonZeroI32>` is "a non-zero i32 might be present"
F * `Result<NonZeroI32, ()>` is "a non-zero i32 success result, if any"
D * `Result<(), NonZeroI32>` is "a non-zero i32 error result, if any"
G [opt-rep]: ../option/index.html#representation "Option Representation"

 Synchronization primitives
 Atomic types
C Atomic types provide primitive shared-memory communication between
9 threads, and are the building blocks of other concurrent
D This module defines atomic versions of a select number of primitive
C types, including [`AtomicBool`], [`AtomicIsize`], [`AtomicUsize`],
" [`AtomicI8`], [`AtomicU16`], etc.
G Atomic types present operations that, when used correctly, synchronize
 updates between threads.
M Atomic variables are safe to share between threads (they implement [`Sync`])
L but they do not themselves provide the mechanism for sharing and follow the
O [threading model](../../../std/thread/index.html#the-threading-model) of Rust.
V The most common way to share an atomic variable is to put it into an [`Arc`][arc] (an
. atomically-reference-counted shared pointer).
) [arc]: ../../../std/sync/struct.Arc.html
B Atomic types may be stored in static variables, initialized using
C the constant initializers like [`AtomicBool::new`]. Atomic statics
/ are often used for lazy global initialization.
$ ## Memory model for atomic accesses
] Rust atomics currently follow the same rules as [C++20 atomics][cpp], specifically the rules
` from the [`intro.races`][cpp-intro.races] section, without the "consume" memory ordering. Since
^ C++ uses an object-based memory model whereas Rust is access-based, a bit of translation work
Y has to be done to apply the C++ rules to Rust: whenever C++ talks about "the value of an
a object", we understand that to mean the resulting bytes obtained when doing a read. When the C++
\ standard talks about "the value of an atomic object", this refers to the result of doing an
_ atomic load (via the operations provided in this module). A "modification of an atomic object"
 refers to an atomic store.
a The end result is *almost* equivalent to saying that creating a *shared reference* to one of the
^ Rust atomic types corresponds to creating an `atomic_ref` in C++, with the `atomic_ref` being
[ destroyed when the lifetime of the shared reference ends. The main difference is that Rust
a permits concurrent atomic and non-atomic reads to the same memory as those cause no issue in the
\ C++ memory model, they are just forbidden in C++ because memory is partitioned into "atomic
` objects" and "non-atomic objects" (with `atomic_ref` temporarily converting a non-atomic object
 into an atomic object).
a The most important aspect of this model is that *data races* are undefined behavior. A data race
Z is defined as conflicting non-synchronized accesses where at least one of the accesses is
a non-atomic. Here, accesses are *conflicting* if they affect overlapping regions of memory and at
] least one of them is a write. (A `compare_exchange` or `compare_exchange_weak` that does not
S succeed is not considered a write.) They are *non-synchronized* if neither of them
W *happens-before* the other, according to the happens-before order of the memory model.
a The other possible cause of undefined behavior in the memory model are mixed-size accesses: Rust
` inherits the C++ limitation that non-synchronized conflicting atomic accesses may not partially
a overlap. In other words, every pair of non-synchronized atomic accesses must be either disjoint,
W access the exact same memory (including using the same access size), or both be reads.
\ Each atomic access takes an [`Ordering`] which defines how the operation interacts with the
Y happens-before order. These orderings behave the same as the corresponding [C++20 atomic
G orderings][cpp_memory_order]. For more information, see the [nomicon].
0 [cpp]: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic
[ [cpp-intro.races]: https://timsong-cpp.github.io/cppwp/n4868/intro.multithread#intro.races
J [cpp_memory_order]: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/memory_order
) [nomicon]: ../../../nomicon/atomics.html
" ```rust,no_run undefined_behavior

 # Portability
L All atomic types in this module are guaranteed to be [lock-free] if they're
K available. This means they don't internally acquire a global mutex. Atomic
I types and operations are not guaranteed to be wait-free. This means that
L operations like `fetch_or` may be implemented with a compare-and-swap loop.
C Atomic operations may be implemented at the instruction layer with
B larger-size atomics. For example some platforms use 4-byte atomic
J instructions to implement `AtomicI8`. Note that this emulation should not
K have an impact on correctness of code, it's just something to be aware of.
M The atomic types in this module might not be available on all platforms. The
J atomic types here are all widely available, however, and can generally be
3 relied upon existing. Some notable exceptions are:
M * PowerPC and MIPS platforms with 32-bit pointers do not have `AtomicU64` or
   `AtomicI64` types.
J * Legacy ARM platforms like ARMv4T and ARMv5TE have very limited hardware
B   support for atomics. The bare-metal targets disable this module
J   entirely, but the Linux targets [use the kernel] to assist (which comes
K   with a performance penalty). It's not until ARMv6K onwards that ARM CPUs
N   have support for load/store and Compare and Swap (CAS) atomics in hardware.
9 * ARMv6-M and ARMv8-M baseline targets (`thumbv6m-*` and
H   `thumbv8m.base-*`) only provide `load` and `store` operations, and do
A   not support Compare and Swap (CAS) operations, such as `swap`,
I   `fetch_add`, etc. Full CAS support is available on ARMv7-M and ARMv8-M
?   Mainline (`thumbv7m-*`, `thumbv7em*` and `thumbv8m.main-*`).
W [use the kernel]: https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/arm/kernel_user_helpers.txt
J Note that future platforms may be added that also do not have support for
H some atomic operations. Maximally portable code will want to be careful
G about which atomic types are used. `AtomicUsize` and `AtomicIsize` are
M generally the most portable, but even then they're not available everywhere.
\ For reference, the `std` library requires `AtomicBool`s and pointer-sized atomics, although
 `core` does not.
G The `#[cfg(target_has_atomic)]` attribute can be used to conditionally
F compile based on the target's supported bit widths. It is a key-value
G option set for each supported size, with values "8", "16", "32", "64",
, "128", and "ptr" for pointer-sized atomics.
B [lock-free]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-blocking_algorithm
& # Atomic accesses to read-only memory
g In general, *all* atomic accesses on read-only memory are undefined behavior. For instance, attempting
Y to do a `compare_exchange` that will definitely fail (making it conceptually a read-only
i operation) can still cause a segmentation fault if the underlying memory page is mapped read-only. Since
_ atomic `load`s might be implemented using compare-exchange operations, even a `load` can fault
 on read-only memory.
^ For the purpose of this section, "read-only memory" is defined as memory that is read-only in
a the underlying target, i.e., the pages are mapped with a read-only flag and any attempt to write
[ will cause a page fault. In particular, an `&u128` reference that points to memory that is
a read-write mapped is *not* considered to point to "read-only memory". In Rust, almost all memory
a is read-write; the only exceptions are memory created by `const` items or `static` items without
[ interior mutability, and memory that was specifically marked as read-only by the operating
# system via platform-specific APIs.
[ As an exception from the general rule stated above, "sufficiently small" atomic loads with
_ `Ordering::Relaxed` are implemented in a way that works on read-only memory, and are hence not
[ undefined behavior. The exact size limit for what makes a load "sufficiently small" varies
 depending on the target:
 | `target_arch` | Size limit |
 |---------------|---------|
h | `x86`, `arm`, `loongarch32`, `mips`, `mips32r6`, `powerpc`, `riscv32`, `sparc`, `hexagon` | 4 bytes |
s | `x86_64`, `aarch64`, `loongarch64`, `mips64`, `mips64r6`, `powerpc64`, `riscv64`, `sparc64`, `s390x` | 8 bytes |
Z Atomics loads that are larger than this limit as well as atomic loads with ordering other
a than `Relaxed`, as well as *all* atomic loads on targets not listed in the table, might still be
` read-only under certain conditions, but that is not a stable guarantee and should not be relied
 upon.
` If you need to do an acquire load on read-only memory, you can do a relaxed load followed by an
 acquire fence instead.

> # Migrating to `compare_exchange` and `compare_exchange_weak`
V `compare_and_swap` is equivalent to `compare_exchange` with the following mapping for
 memory orderings:
 Original | Success | Failure
 -------- | ------- | -------
 Relaxed  | Relaxed | Relaxed
 Acquire  | Acquire | Acquire
 Release  | Release | Relaxed
 AcqRel   | AcqRel  | Acquire
 SeqCst   | SeqCst  | SeqCst
X `compare_and_swap` and `compare_exchange` also differ in their return type. You can use
] `compare_exchange(...).unwrap_or_else(|x| x)` to recover the behavior of `compare_and_swap`,
Z but in most cases it is more idiomatic to check whether the return value is `Ok` or `Err`
J rather than to infer success vs failure based on the value that was read.
Z During migration, consider whether it makes sense to use `compare_exchange_weak` instead.
Y `compare_exchange_weak` is allowed to fail spuriously even when the comparison succeeds,
U which allows the compiler to generate better assembly code when the compare and swap
 is used in a loop.
N assert_eq!(some_bool.compare_and_swap(true, false, Ordering::Relaxed), true);
N assert_eq!(some_bool.compare_and_swap(true, true, Ordering::Relaxed), false);

Z Fences create synchronization between themselves and atomic operations or fences in other
a threads. To achieve this, a fence prevents the compiler and CPU from reordering certain types of
 memory operations around it.
3 There are 3 different ways to use an atomic fence:
[ - atomic - fence synchronization: an atomic operation with (at least) [`Release`] ordering
V   semantics synchronizes with a fence with (at least) [`Acquire`] ordering semantics.
Y - fence - atomic synchronization: a fence with (at least) [`Release`] ordering semantics
X   synchronizes with an atomic operation with (at least) [`Acquire`] ordering semantics.
X - fence - fence synchronization: a fence with (at least) [`Release`] ordering semantics
L   synchronizes with a fence with (at least) [`Acquire`] ordering semantics.
R These 3 ways complement the regular, fence-less, atomic - atomic synchronization.
 ## Atomic - Fence
X An atomic operation on one thread will synchronize with a fence on another thread when:
 -   on thread 1:
^     -   an atomic operation 'X' with (at least) [`Release`] ordering semantics on some atomic
         object 'm',
  -   is paired on thread 2 with:
2     -   an atomic read 'Y' with any order on 'm',
P     -   followed by a fence 'B' with (at least) [`Acquire`] ordering semantics.
; This provides a happens-before dependence between X and B.
?     Thread 1                                          Thread 2
! m.store(3, Release); X ---------
!                                |
K                                -------------> Y  if m.load(Relaxed) == 3 {
E                                               B      fence(Acquire);
9                                                      ...
3                                                  }
 ## Fence - Atomic
X A fence on one thread will synchronize with an atomic operation on another thread when:
 -   on thread:
D     -   a fence 'A' with (at least) [`Release`] ordering semantics,
U     -   followed by an atomic write 'X' with any ordering on some atomic object 'm',
P     -   an atomic operation 'Y' with (at least) [`Acquire`] ordering semantics.
; This provides a happens-before dependence between A and Y.
 fence(Release);      A
! m.store(3, Relaxed); X ---------

 ## Fence - Fence
L A fence on one thread will synchronize with a fence on another thread when:
I     -   a fence 'A' which has (at least) [`Release`] ordering semantics,
5     -   an atomic read 'Y' with any ordering on 'm',
; This provides a happens-before dependence between A and B.
& fence(Release);      A --------------
& m.store(3, Relaxed); X ---------    |
&                                |    |
E                                     |-------> B      fence(Acquire);

` Note that in the examples above, it is crucial that the access to `m` are atomic. Fences cannot
` be used to establish synchronization between non-atomic accesses in different threads. However,
_ thanks to the happens-before relationship, any non-atomic access that happen-before the atomic
X operation or fence with (at least) [`Release`] ordering semantics are now also properly
_ synchronized with any non-atomic accesses that happen-after the atomic operation or fence with
+ (at least) [`Acquire`] ordering semantics.

  A "compiler-only" atomic fence.
[ Like [`fence`], this function establishes synchronization with other atomic operations and
Z fences. However, unlike [`fence`], `compiler_fence` only establishes synchronization with
] operations *in the same thread*. This may at first sound rather useless, since code within a
[ thread is typically already totally ordered and does not need any further synchronization.
V However, there are cases where code can run on the same thread without being ordered:
_ - The most common case is that of a *signal handler*: a signal handler runs in the same thread
`   as the code it interrupted, but it is not ordered with respect to that code. `compiler_fence`
a   can be used to establish synchronization between a thread and its signal handler, the same way
H   that `fence` can be used to establish synchronization across threads.
] - Similar situations can arise in embedded programming with interrupt handlers, or in custom
Z   implementations of preemptive green threads. In general, `compiler_fence` can establish
P   synchronization with code that is guaranteed to run on the same hardware CPU.
Z See [`fence`] for how a fence can be used to achieve synchronization. Note that just like
` [`fence`], synchronization still requires atomic operations to be used in both threads -- it is
X not possible to perform synchronization entirely with fences and non-atomic operations.
_ `compiler_fence` does not emit any machine code, but restricts the kinds of memory re-ordering
` the compiler is allowed to do. `compiler_fence` corresponds to [`atomic_signal_fence`] in C and
 C++.
V [`atomic_signal_fence`]: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/atomic_signal_fence

W thread, and explicit synchronization is required to pass data between a thread and its

F `SyncView` provides _mutable_ access, also referred to as _exclusive_
R access to the underlying value. However, it only permits _immutable_, or _shared_
< access to the underlying value when that value is [`Sync`].
O While this may seem not very useful, it allows `SyncView` to _unconditionally_
V implement `Sync`. Indeed, the safety requirements of `Sync` state that for `SyncView`
T to be `Sync`, it must be sound to _share_ across threads, that is, it must be sound
W for `&SyncView` to cross thread boundaries. By design, a `&SyncView<T>` for non-`Sync`
O `T` has no API whatsoever, making it useless, thus harmless, thus memory safe.
N Certain constructs like [`Future`]s can only be used with _exclusive_ access,
P and are often [`Send`] but not `Sync`, so `SyncView` can be used as hint to the
4 Rust compiler that something is `Sync` in practice.

a It may omit internal state, precision, or other information the type does not consider important
a for user-facing output, as determined by the type. As such, the output of `Display` might not be
a possible to parse, and even if it is, the result of parsing might not exactly match the original
W However, if a type has a lossless `Display` implementation whose output is meant to be
` conveniently machine-parseable and not just meant for human consumption, then the type may wish

 ## `Hash` and `Eq`
M When implementing both `Hash` and [`Eq`], it is important that the following
 property holds:
! k1 == k2 -> hash(k1) == hash(k2)
H In other words, if two keys are equal, their hashes must also be equal.
8 [`HashMap`] and [`HashSet`] both rely on this behavior.
G Thankfully, you won't need to worry about upholding this property when
G deriving both [`Eq`] and `Hash` with `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]`.
 ## Prefix collisions
; Implementations of `hash` should ensure that the data they
/ pass to the `Hasher` are prefix-free. That is,
Y values which are not equal should cause two different sequences of values to be written,
B and neither of the two sequences should be a prefix of the other.
V For example, the standard implementation of [`Hash` for `&str`][impl] passes an extra
H `0xFF` byte to the `Hasher` so that the values `("ab", "c")` and `("a",
 "bc")` hash differently.
R Due to differences in endianness and type sizes, data fed by `Hash` to a `Hasher`
Y should not be considered portable across platforms. Additionally the data passed by most
R standard library types should not be considered stable between compiler versions.
V This means tests shouldn't probe hard-coded hash values or data fed to a `Hasher` and
, instead should check consistency with `Eq`.
\ Serialization formats intended to be portable between platforms or compiler versions should
V either avoid encoding hashes or only rely on `Hash` and `Hasher` implementations that
 provide additional guarantees.

M A `Waker` is a handle for waking up a task by notifying its executor that it

D This handle encapsulates a [`RawWaker`] instance, which defines the
# executor-specific wakeup behavior.
U The typical life of a `Waker` is that it is constructed by an executor, wrapped in a
V [`Context`], then passed to [`Future::poll()`]. Then, if the future chooses to return
X [`Poll::Pending`], it must also store the waker somehow and call [`Waker::wake()`] when
# the future should be polled again.
P Implements [`Clone`], [`Send`], and [`Sync`]; therefore, a waker may be invoked
U from any thread, including ones not in any way managed by the executor. For example,
W this might be done to wake a future when a blocking function call completes on another

J The `GlobalAlloc` trait is an `unsafe` trait for a number of reasons, and
> implementors must ensure that they adhere to these contracts:
L * It's undefined behavior if global allocators unwind. This restriction may
C   be lifted in the future, but currently a panic from any of these
)   functions may lead to memory unsafety.
K * `Layout` queries and calculations in general must be correct. Callers of
J   this trait are allowed to rely on the contracts defined on each method,
;   and implementors must ensure such contracts remain true.
R * You must not rely on allocations actually happening, even if there are explicit
a   heap allocations in the source. The optimizer may detect unused allocations that it can either
S   eliminate entirely or move to the stack and thus never invoke the allocator. The
\   optimizer may further assume that allocation is infallible, so code that used to fail due
V   to allocator failures may now suddenly work because the optimizer worked around the
_   need for an allocation. More concretely, the following code example is unsound, irrespective
W   of whether your custom allocator allows counting how many allocations have happened.
0   ```rust,ignore (unsound and has placeholders)
   drop(Box::new(42));
@   let number_of_heap_allocs = /* call private allocator API */;
E   unsafe { std::hint::assert_unchecked(number_of_heap_allocs > 0); }
?   Note that the optimizations mentioned above are not the only
S   optimization that can be applied. You may generally not rely on heap allocations
F   happening if they can be removed without changing program behavior.
T   Whether allocations happen or not is not part of the program behavior, even if it
V   could be detected via an allocator that tracks allocations by printing or otherwise
   having side effects.

I Returns the result of the `cpuid` instruction for a given `leaf` (`EAX`)
 and `sub_leaf` (`ECX`).
S There are two types of information leaves - basic leaves (with `leaf < 0x8000000`)
Q and extended leaves (with `leaf >= 0x80000000`). The highest supported basic and
L extended leaves can be obtained by calling CPUID with `0` and `0x80000000`,
P respectively, and reading the value in the `EAX` register. If the leaf supports
N more than one sub-leaf, then the procedure of obtaining the highest supported
Q sub-leaf, as well as the behavior if a invalid sub-leaf value is passed, depends
 on the specific leaf.
P If the `leaf` value is higher than the maximum supported basic or extended leaf
P for the processor, this returns the information for the highest supported basic
Q information leaf (with the passed `sub_leaf` value). If the `leaf` value is less
O than or equal to the highest basic or extended leaf value, but the leaf is not
4 supported on the processor, all zeros are returned.
R The [CPUID Wikipedia page][wiki_cpuid] contains information on how to query which
K information using the `EAX` and `ECX` registers, and the interpretation of
8 the results returned in `EAX`, `EBX`, `ECX`, and `EDX`.
 The references are:

[ Performs a serializing operation on all non-temporal ("streaming") store instructions that
= were issued by the current thread prior to this instruction.
d Guarantees that every non-temporal store instruction that precedes this fence, in program order, is
H ordered before any load or store instruction which follows the fence in

r [Intel's documentation](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_sfence)
U (but note that Intel is only documenting the hardware-level concerns related to this
^ instruction; the Intel documentation does not take into account the extra concerns that arise
G because the Rust memory model is different from the x86 memory model.)
  # Safety of non-temporal stores
a After using any non-temporal store intrinsic, but before any other access to the memory that the
X intrinsic mutates, a call to `_mm_sfence` must be performed on the thread that used the
 intrinsic.
[ Non-temporal stores behave very different from regular stores. For the purpose of the Rust
] memory model, these stores are happening asynchronously in a background thread. This means a
] non-temporal store can cause data races with other accesses, even other accesses on the same
a thread. It also means that cross-thread synchronization does not work as expected: let's say the
a intrinsic is called on thread T1, and T1 performs synchronization with some other thread T2. The
a non-temporal store acts as if it happened not in T1 but in a different thread T3, and T2 has not
] synchronized with T3! Calling `_mm_sfence` makes the current thread wait for and synchronize
^ with all the non-temporal stores previously started on this thread, which means in particular
U that subsequent synchronization with other threads will then work as intended again.
] The general pattern to use non-temporal stores correctly is to call `_mm_sfence` before your
[ code jumps back to code outside your library. This ensures all stores inside your function
Y are synchronized-before the return, and thus transitively synchronized-before everything
- the caller does after your function returns.
I Gets the unsigned 32-bit value of the MXCSR control and status register.
X Note that Rust makes no guarantees whatsoever about the contents of this register: Rust
` floating-point operations may or may not result in this register getting updated with exception
Y state, and the register can change between two invocations of this function even when no
_ floating-point operations appear in the source code (since floating-point operations appearing
$ earlier or later can be reordered).
W If you need to perform some floating-point operations and check whether they raised an
O exception, use an inline assembly block for the entire sequence of operations.
5 For more info see [`_mm_setcsr`](fn._mm_setcsr.html)

@ Sets the MXCSR register with the 32-bit unsigned integer value.
C This register controls how SIMD instructions handle floating point
E operations. Modifying this register only affects the current thread.
% It contains several groups of flags:
Q * *Exception flags* report which exceptions occurred since last they were reset.
N * *Masking flags* can be used to mask (ignore) certain exceptions. By default
C   these flags are all set to 1, so all exceptions are masked. When
K   an exception is masked, the processor simply sets the exception flag and
N   continues the operation. If the exception is unmasked, the flag is also set
4   but additionally an exception handler is invoked.
D * *Rounding mode flags* control the rounding mode of floating point
   instructions.
F * The *denormals-are-zero mode flag* turns all numbers which would be
9   denormalized (exponent bits are all zeros) into zeros.
` Note that modifying the masking flags, rounding mode, or denormals-are-zero mode flags leads to
` **immediate Undefined Behavior**: Rust assumes that these are always in their default state and
a will optimize accordingly. This even applies when the register is altered and later reset to its
` original value without any floating-point operations appearing in the source code between those
Z operations (since floating-point operations appearing earlier or later can be reordered).
` If you need to perform some floating-point operations under a different masking flags, rounding
\ mode, or denormals-are-zero mode, use an inline assembly block and make sure to restore the
; original MXCSR register state before the end of the block.
 ## Exception Flags
K * `_MM_EXCEPT_INVALID`: An invalid operation was performed (e.g., dividing
   Infinity by Infinity).
K * `_MM_EXCEPT_DENORM`: An operation attempted to operate on a denormalized
3   number. Mainly this can cause loss of precision.
4 * `_MM_EXCEPT_DIV_ZERO`: Division by zero occurred.
H * `_MM_EXCEPT_OVERFLOW`: A numeric overflow exception occurred, i.e., a
G   result was too large to be represented (e.g., an `f32` with absolute
   value greater than `2^128`).
J * `_MM_EXCEPT_UNDERFLOW`: A numeric underflow exception occurred, i.e., a
G   result was too small to be represented in a normalized way (e.g., an
4   `f32` with absolute value smaller than `2^-126`.)
E * `_MM_EXCEPT_INEXACT`: An inexact-result exception occurred (a.k.a.
L   precision exception). This means some precision was lost due to rounding.
H   For example, the fraction `1/3` cannot be represented accurately in a
G   32 or 64 bit float and computing it would cause this exception to be
L   raised. Precision exceptions are very common, so they are usually masked.
D Exception flags can be read and set using the convenience functions
I `_MM_GET_EXCEPTION_STATE` and `_MM_SET_EXCEPTION_STATE`. For example, to
, check if an operation caused some overflow:
 ```rust,ignore
9 _MM_SET_EXCEPTION_STATE(0); // clear all exception flags
4                             // perform calculations
: if _MM_GET_EXCEPTION_STATE() & _MM_EXCEPT_OVERFLOW != 0 {
     // handle overflow
 ## Masking Flags
G There is one masking flag for each exception flag: `_MM_MASK_INVALID`,
= `_MM_MASK_DENORM`, `_MM_MASK_DIV_ZERO`, `_MM_MASK_OVERFLOW`,
* `_MM_MASK_UNDERFLOW`, `_MM_MASK_INEXACT`.
$ A single masking bit can be set via
, _MM_SET_EXCEPTION_MASK(_MM_MASK_UNDERFLOW);
K However, since mask bits are by default all set to 1, it is more common to
E want to *disable* certain bits. For example, to unmask the underflow

D _mm_setcsr(_mm_getcsr() & !_MM_MASK_UNDERFLOW); // unmask underflow
 exception
E Warning: an unmasked exception will cause an exception handler to be
 called.
I The standard handler will simply terminate the process. So, in this case
K any underflow exception would terminate the current process with something
: like `signal: 8, SIGFPE: erroneous arithmetic operation`.

2 * `_MM_ROUND_UP`: Round toward positive Infinity.

 Round packed single-precision (32-bit) floating-point elements in a to the number of fraction bits specified by imm8, and store the results in dst.\
O Rounding is done according to the imm8\[2:0\] parameter, which can be one of:\
3 * [`_MM_FROUND_TO_NEAREST_INT`] : round to nearest
) * [`_MM_FROUND_TO_NEG_INF`] : round down
' * [`_MM_FROUND_TO_POS_INF`] : round up
$ * [`_MM_FROUND_TO_ZERO`] : truncate

 Normalize the mantissas of packed single-precision (32-bit) floating-point elements in a, and store the results in dst. This intrinsic essentially calculates 
(2^k)*|x.significand|, where k depends on the interval range defined by interv and the sign depends on sc and the source sign.
e The mantissa is normalized to the interval specified by interv, which can take the following values:
,    _MM_MANT_NORM_1_2     // interval [1, 2)
.    _MM_MANT_NORM_p5_2    // interval [0.5, 2)
.    _MM_MANT_NORM_p5_1    // interval [0.5, 1)
1    _MM_MANT_NORM_p75_1p5 // interval [0.75, 1.5)
B The sign is determined by sc which can take the following values:
-    _MM_MANT_SIGN_src     // sign = sign(src)
%    _MM_MANT_SIGN_zero    // sign = 0
7    _MM_MANT_SIGN_nan     // dst = NaN if sign(src) = 1
 [Intel's documentation](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm512_getmant_ps&expand=2880)

 Compute the absolute differences of packed unsigned 8-bit integers in a and b, then horizontally sum each consecutive 8 differences to produce eight unsigned 16-bit integers, and pack these unsigned 16-bit integers in the low 16 bits of 64-bit elements in dst.
 [Intel's documentation](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm512_sad_epu8&expand=4855)
 Compute the sum of absolute differences (SADs) of quadruplets of unsigned 8-bit integers in a compared to those in b, and store the 16-bit results in dst. Four SADs are performed on four 8-bit quadruplets for each 64-bit lane. The first two SADs use the lower 8-bit quadruplet of the lane from a, and the last two SADs use the uppper 8-bit quadruplet of the lane from a. Quadruplets from b are selected from within 128-bit lanes according to the control in imm8, and each SAD in each 64-bit lane uses the selected quadruplet at 8-bit offsets.

f Load internal wrapping key (IWKey). The 32-bit unsigned integer `control` specifies IWKey's KeySource
d and whether backing up the key is permitted. IWKey's 256-bit encryption key is loaded from `key_lo`
 and `key_hi`.
F  - `control[0]`: NoBackup bit. If set, the IWKey cannot be backed up.
a  - `control[1:4]`: KeySource bits. These bits specify the encoding method of the IWKey. The only
c    allowed values are `0` (AES GCM SIV wrapping algorithm with the specified key) and `1` (AES GCM
e    SIV wrapping algorithm with random keys enforced by hardware). After calling `_mm_loadiwkey` with
b    KeySource set to `1`, software must check `ZF` to ensure that the key was loaded successfully.
G    Using any other value may result in a General Protection Exception.
A  - `control[5:31]`: Reserved for future use, must be set to `0`.
f Note that setting the NoBackup bit and using the KeySource value `1` requires hardware support. These
h permissions can be found by calling `__cpuid(0x19)` and checking the `ECX[0:1]` bits. Failing to follow
A these restrictions may result in a General Protection Exception.
u [Intel's documentation](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm_loadiwkey)
b Wrap a 128-bit AES key into a 384-bit key handle and stores it in `handle`. Returns the `control`
$ parameter used to create the IWKey.
E  - `key_params[0]`: If set, this key can only be used by the Kernel.
A  - `key_params[1]`: If set, this key can not be used to encrypt.
A  - `key_params[2]`: If set, this key can not be used to decrypt.
D  - `key_params[31:3]`: Reserved for future use, must be set to `0`.
c Note that these restrictions need hardware support, and the supported restrictions can be found by
c calling `__cpuid(0x19)` and checking the `EAX[0:2]` bits. Failing to follow these restrictions may
* result in a General Protection Exception.

> Compares and exchange 16 bytes (128 bits) of data atomically.
G This intrinsic corresponds to the `cmpxchg16b` instruction on `x86_64`
G processors. It performs an atomic compare-and-swap, updating the `ptr`
F memory location to `val` if the current value in memory equals `old`.
J This function returns the previous value at the memory location. If it is
5 equal to `old` then the memory was updated to `new`.
 # Memory Orderings
D This atomic operation has the same semantics of memory orderings as
K `AtomicUsize::compare_exchange` does, only operating on 16 bytes of memory
 instead of just a pointer.
L The failure ordering must be [`Ordering::SeqCst`], [`Ordering::Acquire`] or
 [`Ordering::Relaxed`].
I For more information on memory orderings here see the `compare_exchange`
A documentation for other `Atomic*` types in the standard library.
 # Unsafety
I This method is unsafe because it takes a raw pointer and will attempt to
L read and possibly write the memory at the pointer. The pointer must also be
 aligned on a 16-byte boundary.
J This method also requires the `cmpxchg16b` CPU feature to be available at
K runtime to work correctly. If the CPU running the binary does not actually
C support `cmpxchg16b` and the program enters an execution path that
@ eventually would reach this function the behavior is undefined.

`SIMD and vendor intrinsics module.
This module is intended to be the gateway to architecture-specific
intrinsic functions, typically related to SIMD (but not always!). Each
architecture that Rust compiles to may contain a submodule here, which
means that this is not a portable module! If you're writing a portable
library take care when using these APIs!
Under this module you'll find an architecture-named module, such as
`x86_64`. Each `#[cfg(target_arch)]` that Rust can compile to may have a
module entry here, only present on that particular target. For example the
`i686-pc-windows-msvc` target will have an `x86` module here, whereas
`x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` has `x86_64`.
[rfc]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2325
[tracked]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/48556
# Overview
This module exposes vendor-specific intrinsics that typically correspond to
a single machine instruction. These intrinsics are not portable: their
availability is architecture-dependent, and not all machines of that
architecture might provide the intrinsic.
The `arch` module is intended to be a low-level implementation detail for
higher-level APIs. Using it correctly can be quite tricky as you need to
ensure at least a few guarantees are upheld:
* The correct architecture's module is used. For example the `arm` module
  isn't available on the `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` target. This is
  typically done by ensuring that `#[cfg]` is used appropriately when using
  this module.
* The CPU the program is currently running on supports the function being
  called. For example it is unsafe to call an AVX2 function on a CPU that
  doesn't actually support AVX2.
As a result of the latter of these guarantees all intrinsics in this module
are `unsafe` and extra care needs to be taken when calling them!
# CPU Feature Detection
In order to call these APIs in a safe fashion there's a number of
mechanisms available to ensure that the correct CPU feature is available
to call an intrinsic. Let's consider, for example, the `_mm256_add_epi64`
intrinsics on the `x86` and `x86_64` architectures. This function requires
the AVX2 feature as [documented by Intel][intel-dox] so to correctly call
this function we need to (a) guarantee we only call it on `x86`/`x86_64`
and (b) ensure that the CPU feature is available
[intel-dox]: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#text=_mm256_add_epi64&expand=100
## Static CPU Feature Detection
The first option available to us is to conditionally compile code via the
`#[cfg]` attribute. CPU features correspond to the `target_feature` cfg
available, and can be used like so:
```ignore
#[cfg(
    all(
        any(target_arch = "x86", target_arch = "x86_64"),
        target_feature = "avx2"
    )
fn foo() {
    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86")]
    use std::arch::x86::_mm256_add_epi64;
    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
    use std::arch::x86_64::_mm256_add_epi64;
    unsafe {
        _mm256_add_epi64(...);
    }
Here we're using `#[cfg(target_feature = "avx2")]` to conditionally compile
this function into our module. This means that if the `avx2` feature is
*enabled statically* then we'll use the `_mm256_add_epi64` function at
runtime. The `unsafe` block here can be justified through the usage of
`#[cfg]` to only compile the code in situations where the safety guarantees
are upheld.
Statically enabling a feature is typically done with the `-C
target-feature` or `-C target-cpu` flags to the compiler. For example if
your local CPU supports AVX2 then you can compile the above function with:
```sh
$ RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build
Or otherwise you can specifically enable just the AVX2 feature:
```sh
$ RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' cargo build
Note that when you compile a binary with a particular feature enabled it's
important to ensure that you only run the binary on systems which satisfy
the required feature set.
## Dynamic CPU Feature Detection
Sometimes statically dispatching isn't quite what you want. Instead you
might want to build a portable binary that runs across a variety of CPUs,
but at runtime it selects the most optimized implementation available. This
allows you to build a "least common denominator" binary which has certain
sections more optimized for different CPUs.
Taking our previous example from before, we're going to compile our binary
*without* AVX2 support, but we'd like to enable it for just one function.
We can do that in a manner like:
```ignore
fn foo() {
    #[cfg(any(target_arch = "x86", target_arch = "x86_64"))]
    {
        if is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2") {
            return unsafe { foo_avx2() };
        }
    }
    // fallback implementation without using AVX2
#[cfg(any(target_arch = "x86", target_arch = "x86_64"))]
#[target_feature(enable = "avx2")]
unsafe fn foo_avx2() {
    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86")]
    use std::arch::x86::_mm256_add_epi64;
    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
    use std::arch::x86_64::_mm256_add_epi64;
    unsafe { _mm256_add_epi64(...); }
There's a couple of components in play here, so let's go through them in
detail!
* First up we notice the `is_x86_feature_detected!` macro. Provided by
  the standard library, this macro will perform necessary runtime detection
  to determine whether the CPU the program is running on supports the
  specified feature. In this case the macro will expand to a boolean
  expression evaluating to whether the local CPU has the AVX2 feature or
  not.
  Note that this macro, like the `arch` module, is platform-specific. For
  example calling `is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")` on ARM will be a
  compile time error. To ensure we don't hit this error a statement level
  `#[cfg]` is used to only compile usage of the macro on `x86`/`x86_64`.
* Next up we see our AVX2-enabled function, `foo_avx2`. This function is
  decorated with the `#[target_feature]` attribute which enables a CPU
  feature for just this one function. Using a compiler flag like `-C
  target-feature=+avx2` will enable AVX2 for the entire program, but using
  an attribute will only enable it for the one function. Usage of the
  `#[target_feature]` attribute currently requires the function to also be
  `unsafe`, as we see here. This is because the function can only be
  correctly called on systems which have the AVX2 (like the intrinsics
  themselves).
And with all that we should have a working program! This program will run
across all machines and it'll use the optimized AVX2 implementation on
machines where support is detected.
# Ergonomics
It's important to note that using the `arch` module is not the easiest
thing in the world, so if you're curious to try it out you may want to
brace yourself for some wordiness!
The primary purpose of this module is to enable stable crates on crates.io
to build up much more ergonomic abstractions which end up using SIMD under
the hood. Over time these abstractions may also move into the standard
library itself, but for now this module is tasked with providing the bare
minimum necessary to use vendor intrinsics on stable Rust.

Next up let's take a look at an example of manually using intrinsics. Here
we'll be using SSE4.1 features to implement hex encoding.
fn main() {
    let mut dst = [0; 32];
    hex_encode(b"\x01\x02\x03", &mut dst);
    assert_eq!(&dst[..6], b"010203");
    let mut src = [0; 16];
    for i in 0..16 {
        src[i] = (i + 1) as u8;
    }
    hex_encode(&src, &mut dst);
    assert_eq!(&dst, b"0102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f10");
pub fn hex_encode(src: &[u8], dst: &mut [u8]) {
    let len = src.len().checked_mul(2).unwrap();
    assert!(dst.len() >= len);
    #[cfg(any(target_arch = "x86", target_arch = "x86_64"))]
    {
        if is_x86_feature_detected!("sse4.1") {
            return unsafe { hex_encode_sse41(src, dst) };
        }
    }
    hex_encode_fallback(src, dst)
// translated from
// <https://github.com/Matherunner/bin2hex-sse/blob/master/base16_sse4.cpp>
#[target_feature(enable = "sse4.1")]
#[cfg(any(target_arch = "x86", target_arch = "x86_64"))]
unsafe fn hex_encode_sse41(mut src: &[u8], dst: &mut [u8]) {
    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86")]
    use std::arch::x86::*;
    #[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]
    use std::arch::x86_64::*;
    unsafe {
        let ascii_zero = _mm_set1_epi8(b'0' as i8);
        let nines = _mm_set1_epi8(9);
        let ascii_a = _mm_set1_epi8((b'a' - 9 - 1) as i8);
        let and4bits = _mm_set1_epi8(0xf);
        let mut i = 0_isize;
        while src.len() >= 16 {
            let invec = _mm_loadu_si128(src.as_ptr() as *const _);
            let masked1 = _mm_and_si128(invec, and4bits);
            let masked2 = _mm_and_si128(_mm_srli_epi64(invec, 4), and4bits);
            // return 0xff corresponding to the elements > 9, or 0x00 otherwise
            let cmpmask1 = _mm_cmpgt_epi8(masked1, nines);
            let cmpmask2 = _mm_cmpgt_epi8(masked2, nines);
            // add '0' or the offset depending on the masks
            let masked1 = _mm_add_epi8(
                masked1,
                _mm_blendv_epi8(ascii_zero, ascii_a, cmpmask1),
            );
            let masked2 = _mm_add_epi8(
                masked2,
                _mm_blendv_epi8(ascii_zero, ascii_a, cmpmask2),
            );
            // interleave masked1 and masked2 bytes
            let res1 = _mm_unpacklo_epi8(masked2, masked1);
            let res2 = _mm_unpackhi_epi8(masked2, masked1);
            _mm_storeu_si128(dst.as_mut_ptr().offset(i * 2) as *mut _, res1);
            _mm_storeu_si128(
                dst.as_mut_ptr().offset(i * 2 + 16) as *mut _,
                res2,
            );
            src = &src[16..];
            i += 16;
        }
        let i = i as usize;
        hex_encode_fallback(src, &mut dst[i * 2..]);
    }
fn hex_encode_fallback(src: &[u8], dst: &mut [u8]) {
    fn hex(byte: u8) -> u8 {
        static TABLE: &[u8] = b"0123456789abcdef";
        TABLE[byte as usize]
    }
    for (byte, slots) in src.iter().zip(dst.chunks_mut(2)) {
        slots[0] = hex((*byte >> 4) & 0xf);
        slots[1] = hex(*byte & 0xf);
    }

 The `core::arch::return_address!()` macro returns a pointer with an address that corresponds to the caller of the function that invoked the `return_address!()` macro.
 The pointer has no provenance, as if created by `core::ptr::without_provenance`. It cannot be used to read memory (other than ZSTs).
m The value returned by the macro depends highly on the architecture and compiler (including any options set).
s In particular, it is allowed to be wrong (particularly if inlining is involved), or even contain a nonsense value.
l The result of this macro must not be relied upon for soundness or correctness, only for debugging purposes.
s As a best effort, if a useful value cannot be determined (for example, due to limitations on the current codegen),
u this macro tries to return a null pointer instead of nonsense (this cannot be relied upon for correctness, however).
^ Formally, this function returns a pointer with a non-deterministic address and no provenance.
x This is equivalent to the gcc `__builtin_return_address(0)` intrinsic (other forms of the intrinsic are not supported).
 Because the operation can be always performed by the compiler without crashing or causing undefined behaviour, invoking the macro is a safe operation.

D A SIMD vector with the shape of `[T; N]` but the operations of `T`.
Y `Simd<T, N>` supports the operators (+, *, etc.) that `T` does in "elementwise" fashion.
R These take the element at each index from the left-hand side and right-hand side,
[ perform the operation, then return the result in the same index in a vector of equal size.
A However, `Simd` differs from normal iteration and normal arrays:
I - `Simd<T, N>` executes `N` operations in a single step with no `break`s
V - `Simd<T, N>` can have an alignment greater than `T`, for better mechanical sympathy
_ By always imposing these constraints on `Simd`, it is easier to compile elementwise operations
G into machine instructions that can themselves be executed in parallel.
 # use core::simd::{Simd};
 # use core::array;

+ let sum = array::from_fn(|i| a[i] + b[i]);
, let prod = array::from_fn(|i| a[i] * b[i]);

- let (v, w) = (Simd::from(a), Simd::from(b));

Z `Simd` with integer elements treats operators as wrapping, as if `T` was [`Wrapping<T>`].
V Thus, `Simd` does not implement `wrapping_add`, because that is the default behavior.
E This means there is no warning on overflows, even in "debug" builds.
N For most applications where `Simd` is appropriate, it is "not a bug" to wrap,
J and even "debug builds" are unlikely to tolerate the loss of performance.
R You may want to consider using explicitly checked arithmetic if such is required.
6 Division by zero on integers still causes a panic, so
G you may want to consider using `f32` or `f64` if that is unacceptable.
% [`Wrapping<T>`]: core::num::Wrapping
^ `Simd<T, N>` has a layout similar to `[T; N]` (identical "shapes"), with a greater alignment.
_ `[T; N]` is aligned to `T`, but `Simd<T, N>` will have an alignment based on both `T` and `N`.
_ Thus it is sound to [`transmute`] `Simd<T, N>` to `[T; N]` and should optimize to "zero cost",
S but the reverse transmutation may require a copy the compiler cannot simply elide.
R `N` cannot be 0 and may be at most 64. This limit may be increased in the future.
 # ABI "Features"
[ Due to Rust's safety guarantees, `Simd<T, N>` is currently passed and returned via memory,
Z not SIMD registers, except as an optimization. Using `#[inline]` on functions that accept
R `Simd<T, N>` or return it is recommended, at the cost of code generation time, as
R inlining SIMD-using functions can omit a large function prolog or epilog and thus
T improve both speed and code size. The need for this may be corrected in the future.
: Using `#[inline(always)]` still requires additional care.
 # Safe SIMD with Unsafe Rust
r Operations with `Simd` are typically safe, but there are many reasons to want to combine SIMD with `unsafe` code.
u Care must be taken to respect differences between `Simd` and other types it may be transformed into or derived from.
i In particular, the layout of `Simd<T, N>` may be similar to `[T; N]`, and may allow some transmutations,
O but references to `[T; N]` are not interchangeable with those to `Simd<T, N>`.
z Thus, when using `unsafe` Rust to read and write `Simd<T, N>` through [raw pointers], it is a good idea to first try with
= [`read_unaligned`] and [`write_unaligned`]. This is because:
Y - [`read`] and [`write`] require full alignment (in this case, `Simd<T, N>`'s alignment)
^ - `Simd<T, N>` is often read from or written to [`[T]`](slice) and other types aligned to `T`
W - combining these actions violates the `unsafe` contract and explodes the program into
#   a puff of **undefined behavior**
] - the compiler can implicitly adjust layouts to make unaligned reads or writes fully aligned
   if it sees the optimization
Z - most contemporary processors with "aligned" and "unaligned" read and write instructions
U   exhibit no performance difference if the "unaligned" variant is aligned at runtime
^ Less obligations mean unaligned reads and writes are less likely to make the program unsound,
2 and may be just as fast as stricter alternatives.
O When trying to guarantee alignment, [`[T]::as_simd`][as_simd] is an option for
Z converting `[T]` to `[Simd<T, N>]`, and allows soundly operating on an aligned SIMD body,
B but it may cost more time when handling the scalar head and tail.
Z If these are not enough, it is most ideal to design data structures to be already aligned
K to `align_of::<Simd<T, N>>()` before using `unsafe` Rust to read or write.
_ Other ways to compensate for these facts, like materializing `Simd` to or from an array first,
P are handled by safe methods like [`Simd::from_array`] and [`Simd::from_slice`].

Portable SIMD module.
This module offers a portable abstraction for SIMD operations
that is not bound to any particular hardware architecture.
# What is "portable"?
This module provides a SIMD implementation that is fast and predictable on any target.
### Portable SIMD works on every target
Unlike target-specific SIMD in `std::arch`, portable SIMD compiles for every target.
In this regard, it is just like "regular" Rust.
### Portable SIMD is consistent between targets
A program using portable SIMD can expect identical behavior on any target.
In most regards, [`Simd<T, N>`] can be thought of as a parallelized `[T; N]` and operates like a sequence of `T`.
This has one notable exception: a handful of older architectures (e.g. `armv7` and `powerpc`) flush [subnormal](`f32::is_subnormal`) `f32` values to zero.
On these architectures, subnormal `f32` input values are replaced with zeros, and any operation producing subnormal `f32` values produces zeros instead.
This doesn't affect most architectures or programs.
### Operations use the best instructions available
Operations provided by this module compile to the best available SIMD instructions.
Portable SIMD is not a low-level vendor library, and operations in portable SIMD _do not_ necessarily map to a single instruction.
Instead, they map to a reasonable implementation of the operation for the target.
Consistency between targets is not compromised to use faster or fewer instructions.
In some cases, `std::arch` will provide a faster function that has slightly different behavior than the `std::simd` equivalent.
For example, `_mm_min_ps`[^1] can be slightly faster than [`SimdFloat::simd_min`](`num::SimdFloat::simd_min`), but does not conform to the IEEE standard also used by [`f32::min`].
When necessary, [`Simd<T, N>`] can be converted to the types provided by `std::arch` to make use of target-specific functions.
Many targets simply don't have SIMD, or don't support SIMD for a particular element type.
In those cases, regular scalar operations are generated instead.
[^1]: `_mm_min_ps(x, y)` is equivalent to `x.simd_lt(y).select(x, y)`

2 Provides intentionally-wrapped arithmetic on `T`.
B code explicitly expects and relies upon modular arithmetic (e.g.,
 hashing).
@ Wrapping arithmetic can be achieved either through methods like
C `wrapping_add`, or through the `Wrapping<T>` type, which says that
% intended to have wrapping semantics.
 `Wrapping` tuple.
 let zero = Wrapping(0u32);
 let one = Wrapping(1u32);
& assert_eq!(u32::MAX, (zero - one).0);
D `Wrapping<T>` is guaranteed to have the same layout and ABI as `T`.

 # Initialization invariant
a The compiler, in general, assumes that a variable is [properly initialized or "valid"][validity]
Q according to the requirements of the variable's type. For example, a variable of
L reference type must be aligned and non-null. This is an invariant that must
O *always* be upheld, even in unsafe code. As a consequence, zero-initializing a
D variable of reference type causes instantaneous undefined behavior,
B no matter whether that reference ever gets used to access memory:
# use std::mem::{self, MaybeUninit};
F let x: &i32 = unsafe { mem::zeroed() }; // undefined behavior! 
1 // The equivalent code with `MaybeUninit<&i32>`:
\ let x: &i32 = unsafe { MaybeUninit::zeroed().assume_init() }; // undefined behavior! 
M This is exploited by the compiler for various optimizations, such as eliding
. run-time checks and optimizing `enum` layout.
S Similarly, entirely uninitialized memory may have any content, while a `bool` must
\ always be `true` or `false`. Hence, creating an uninitialized `bool` is undefined behavior:
M let b: bool = unsafe { mem::uninitialized() }; // undefined behavior! 
1 // The equivalent code with `MaybeUninit<bool>`:
\ let b: bool = unsafe { MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() }; // undefined behavior! 
Z Moreover, uninitialized memory is special in that it does not have a fixed value ("fixed"
Y meaning "it won't change without being written to"). Reading the same uninitialized byte
T multiple times can give different results. This makes it undefined behavior to have
` uninitialized data in a variable even if that variable has an integer type, which otherwise can
 hold any *fixed* bit pattern:
L let x: i32 = unsafe { mem::uninitialized() }; // undefined behavior! 
0 // The equivalent code with `MaybeUninit<i32>`:
R Conversely, sometimes it is okay to not initialize *all* bytes of a `MaybeUninit`
Y before calling `assume_init`. For instance, padding bytes do not have to be initialized.
O See the field-by-field struct initialization example below for a case of that.
O `MaybeUninit<T>` serves to enable unsafe code to deal with uninitialized data.
I It is a signal to the compiler indicating that the data here might *not*
 be initialized:
U // Create an explicitly uninitialized reference. The compiler knows that data inside
@ // a `MaybeUninit<T>` may be invalid, and hence this is not UB:
+ let mut x = MaybeUninit::<&i32>::uninit();
 // Set it to a valid value.
 x.write(&0);
I // Extract the initialized data -- this is only allowed *after* properly
 // initializing `x`!
] The compiler then knows to not make any incorrect assumptions or optimizations on this code.
N You can think of `MaybeUninit<T>` as being a bit like `Option<T>` but without
C any of the run-time tracking and without any of the safety checks.

 # Layout is subject to change
= Note that type layout is, in general, [subject to change and
M platform-specific](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-layout.html). If
M layout stability is required, consider using an [explicit `repr` attribute].
N Rust guarantees that the offset of a given field within a given type will not
P change over the lifetime of the program. However, two different compilations of
M the same program may result in different layouts. Also, even within a single
N program execution, no guarantees are made about types which are *similar* but
 not *identical*, e.g.:

 type A = Wrapper<u8, u8>;
 type B = Wrapper<u8, i8>;
M // Not necessarily identical even though `u8` and `i8` have the same layout!
= // assert_eq!(mem::offset_of!(A, 1), mem::offset_of!(B, 1));

M // Not necessarily identical even though `u8` and `U8` have the same layout!
= // assert_eq!(mem::offset_of!(A, 1), mem::offset_of!(C, 1));
/ struct Empty<T>(core::marker::PhantomData<T>);
S // Not necessarily identical even though `PhantomData` always has the same layout!
M // assert_eq!(mem::offset_of!(Empty<u8>, 0), mem::offset_of!(Empty<i8>, 0));
