3 Trait for comparisons using the equality operator.
K Implementing this trait for types provides the `==` and `!=` operators for
 those types.
O `x.eq(y)` can also be written `x == y`, and `x.ne(y)` can be written `x != y`.
Q We use the easier-to-read infix notation in the remainder of this documentation.
I This trait allows for comparisons using the equality operator, for types
M that do not have a full equivalence relation. For example, in floating point
L numbers `NaN != NaN`, so floating point types implement `PartialEq` but not
L [`trait@Eq`]. Formally speaking, when `Rhs == Self`, this trait corresponds
% to a [partial equivalence relation].
[ [partial equivalence relation]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_equivalence_relation
O Implementations must ensure that `eq` and `ne` are consistent with each other:
' - `a != b` if and only if `!(a == b)`.
K The default implementation of `ne` provides this consistency and is almost
I always sufficient. It should not be overridden without very good reason.
` If [`PartialOrd`] or [`Ord`] are also implemented for `Self` and `Rhs`, their methods must also
T be consistent with `PartialEq` (see the documentation of those traits for the exact
_ requirements). It's easy to accidentally make them disagree by deriving some of the traits and
 manually implementing others.
A The equality relation `==` must satisfy the following conditions
/ (for all `a`, `b`, `c` of type `A`, `B`, `C`):
L - **Symmetry**: if `A: PartialEq<B>` and `B: PartialEq<A>`, then **`a == b`
   implies `b == a`**; and
G - **Transitivity**: if `A: PartialEq<B>` and `B: PartialEq<C>` and `A:
B   PartialEq<C>`, then **`a == b` and `b == c` implies `a == c`**.
\   This must also work for longer chains, such as when `A: PartialEq<B>`, `B: PartialEq<C>`,
6   `C: PartialEq<D>`, and `A: PartialEq<D>` all exist.
B Note that the `B: PartialEq<A>` (symmetric) and `A: PartialEq<C>`
I (transitive) impls are not forced to exist, but these requirements apply
 whenever they do exist.
 ## Cross-crate considerations
` Upholding the requirements stated above can become tricky when one crate implements `PartialEq`
` for a type of another crate (i.e., to allow comparing one of its own types with a type from the
^ standard library). The recommendation is to never implement this trait for a foreign type. In
_ other words, such a crate should do `impl PartialEq<ForeignType> for LocalType`, but it should
6 *not* do `impl PartialEq<LocalType> for ForeignType`.
^ This avoids the problem of transitive chains that criss-cross crate boundaries: for all local
a types `T`, you may assume that no other crate will add `impl`s that allow comparing `T == U`. In
a other words, if other crates add `impl`s that allow building longer transitive chains `U1 == ...
^ == T == V1 == ...`, then all the types that appear to the right of `T` must be types that the
a crate defining `T` already knows about. This rules out transitive chains where downstream crates
] can add new `impl`s that "stitch together" comparisons of foreign types in ways that violate
 transitivity.
` Not having such foreign `impl`s also avoids forward compatibility issues where one crate adding
P more `PartialEq` implementations can cause build failures in downstream crates.
H This trait can be used with `#[derive]`. When `derive`d on structs, two
I instances are equal if all fields are equal, and not equal if any fields
H are not equal. When `derive`d on enums, two instances are equal if they
/ are the same variant and all fields are equal.

U which pinning otherwise offers, even when "pinned" by a [`Pin<Ptr>`] pointing at it.

a [repr-rust]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-layout.html#r-layout.repr.rust.unspecified
 # Danger of Improper Variance
G You might think that subtyping is impossible between two static types,
E but this is false; there exists a static type with a static subtype.
F To wit, `fn(&str)`, which is short for `for<'any> fn(&'any str)`, and
= `fn(&'static str)`, are two distinct, static types, and yet,
G `fn(&str)` is a subtype of `fn(&'static str)`, since any value of type
K `fn(&str)` can be used where a value of type `fn(&'static str)` is needed.
: This means that abstractions around `TypeId`, despite its
D `'static` bound on arguments, still need to worry about unnecessary
@ and improper variance: it is advisable to strive for invariance
D first. The usability impact will be negligible, while the reduction
1 in the risk of unsoundness will be most welcome.

> One of the 128 Unicode characters from U+0000 through U+007F,
# often known as the [ASCII] subset.
A Officially, this is the first [block] in Unicode, _Basic Latin_.
H For details, see the [*C0 Controls and Basic Latin*][chart] code chart.
E This block was based on older 7-bit character code standards such as
3 ANSI X3.4-1977, ISO 646-1973, and [NIST FIPS 1-2].
 # When to use this
M The main advantage of this subset is that it's always valid UTF-8.  As such,
M the `&[ascii::Char]` -> `&str` conversion function (as well as other related
0 ones) are O(1): *no* runtime checks are needed.
H If you're consuming strings, you should usually handle Unicode and thus
5 accept `str`s, not limit yourself to `ascii::Char`s.
J However, certain formats are intentionally designed to produce ASCII-only
J output in order to be 8-bit-clean.  In those cases, it can be simpler and
M faster to generate `ascii::Char`s instead of dealing with the variable width
M properties of general UTF-8 encoded strings, while still allowing the result
F to be used freely with other Rust things that deal in general `str`s.
D For example, a UUID library might offer a way to produce the string
C representation of a UUID as an `[ascii::Char; 36]` to avoid memory
G allocation yet still allow it to be used as UTF-8 via `as_str` without
H paying for validation (or needing `unsafe` code) the way it would if it
 were provided as a `[u8; 36]`.
@ This type is guaranteed to have a size and alignment of 1 byte.

Equivalent to C's `char` type.
[C's `char` type] is completely unlike [Rust's `char` type]; while Rust's type represents a unicode scalar value, C's `char` type is just an ordinary integer. On modern architectures this type will always be either [`i8`] or [`u8`], as they use byte-addressed memory with 8-bit bytes.
C chars are most commonly used to make C strings. Unlike Rust, where the length of a string is included alongside the string, C strings mark the end of a string with the character `'\0'`. See `CStr` for more information.
[C's `char` type]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_data_types#Basic_types
[Rust's `char` type]: char
Equivalent to C's `signed char` type.
This type will always be [`i8`], but is included for completeness. It is defined as being a signed integer the same size as a C [`char`].
[`char`]: c_char
Equivalent to C's `unsigned char` type.
This type will always be [`u8`], but is included for completeness. It is defined as being an unsigned integer the same size as a C [`char`].
[`char`]: c_char
Equivalent to C's `signed short` (`short`) type.
This type will almost always be [`i16`], but may differ on some esoteric systems. The C standard technically only requires that this type be a signed integer with at least 16 bits; some systems may define it as `i32`, for example.
Equivalent to C's `unsigned short` type.
This type will almost always be [`u16`], but may differ on some esoteric systems. The C standard technically only requires that this type be an unsigned integer with the same size as a [`short`].
[`short`]: c_short
Equivalent to C's `signed int` (`int`) type.
This type will almost always be [`i32`], but may differ on some esoteric systems. The C standard technically only requires that this type be a signed integer that is at least the size of a [`short`]; some systems define it as an [`i16`], for example.
[`short`]: c_short
Equivalent to C's `unsigned int` type.
This type will almost always be [`u32`], but may differ on some esoteric systems. The C standard technically only requires that this type be an unsigned integer with the same size as an [`int`]; some systems define it as a [`u16`], for example.
[`int`]: c_int
Equivalent to C's `signed long` (`long`) type.
This type will always be [`i32`] or [`i64`]. Most notably, many Linux-based systems assume an `i64`, but Windows assumes `i32`. The C standard technically only requires that this type be a signed integer that is at least 32 bits and at least the size of an [`int`], although in practice, no system would have a `long` that is neither an `i32` nor `i64`.
[`int`]: c_int
Equivalent to C's `unsigned long` type.
This type will always be [`u32`] or [`u64`]. Most notably, many Linux-based systems assume an `u64`, but Windows assumes `u32`. The C standard technically only requires that this type be an unsigned integer with the size of a [`long`], although in practice, no system would have a `ulong` that is neither a `u32` nor `u64`.
[`long`]: c_long
Equivalent to C's `signed long long` (`long long`) type.
This type will almost always be [`i64`], but may differ on some systems. The C standard technically only requires that this type be a signed integer that is at least 64 bits and at least the size of a [`long`], although in practice, no system would have a `long long` that is not an `i64`, as most systems do not have a standardised [`i128`] type.
[`long`]: c_long
Equivalent to C's `unsigned long long` type.
This type will almost always be [`u64`], but may differ on some systems. The C standard technically only requires that this type be an unsigned integer with the size of a [`long long`], although in practice, no system would have a `long long` that is not a `u64`, as most systems do not have a standardised [`u128`] type.
[`long long`]: c_longlong
Equivalent to C's `float` type.
This type will almost always be [`f32`], which is guaranteed to be an [IEEE 754 single-precision float] in Rust. That said, the standard technically only guarantees that it be a floating-point number, and it may have less precision than `f32` or not follow the IEEE-754 standard at all.
[IEEE 754 single-precision float]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754
Equivalent to C's `double` type.
This type will almost always be [`f64`], which is guaranteed to be an [IEEE 754 double-precision float] in Rust. That said, the standard technically only guarantees that it be a floating-point number with at least the precision of a [`float`]; some 16-bit systems use [`f32`], for example. Esoteric systems could use something entirely different from the IEEE-754 standard.
[IEEE 754 double-precision float]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754

. # Handling errors and matching on `ErrorKind`
D In application code, use `match` for the `ErrorKind` values you are
0 expecting; use `_` to match "all other errors".
L In comprehensive and thorough tests that want to verify that a test doesn't
I return any known incorrect error kind, you may want to cut-and-paste the
J current full list of errors from here into your test code, and then match
L `_` as the correct case. This seems counterintuitive, but it will make your
L tests more robust. In particular, if you want to verify that your code does
L produce an unrecognized error kind, the robust solution is to check for all
4 the recognized error kinds and fail in those cases.

 # Notes about side effects
F The [`map`] iterator implements [`DoubleEndedIterator`], meaning that
  you can also [`map`] backwards:
H let v: Vec<i32> = [1, 2, 3].into_iter().map(|x| x + 1).rev().collect();
 assert_eq!(v, [4, 3, 2]);
8 [`DoubleEndedIterator`]: trait.DoubleEndedIterator.html
K But if your closure has state, iterating backwards may act in a way you do
J not expect. Let's go through an example. First, in the forward direction:
 let mut c = 0;
( for pair in ['a', 'b', 'c'].into_iter()

 # Embedding IPv4 Addresses
s To assist in the transition from IPv4 to IPv6 two types of IPv6 addresses that embed an IPv4 address were defined:
o IPv4-compatible and IPv4-mapped addresses. Of these IPv4-compatible addresses have been officially deprecated.
U Both types of addresses are not assigned any special meaning by this implementation,
f other than what the relevant standards prescribe. This means that an address like `::ffff:127.0.0.1`,
d while representing an IPv4 loopback address, is not itself an IPv6 loopback address; only `::1` is.
u To handle these so called "IPv4-in-IPv6" addresses, they have to first be converted to their canonical IPv4 address.
# ### IPv4-Compatible IPv6 Addresses
t IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses are defined in [IETF RFC 4291 Section 2.5.5.1], and have been officially deprecated.
N The RFC describes the format of an "IPv4-Compatible IPv6 address" as follows:
D |                80 bits               | 16 |      32 bits        |
D +--------------------------------------+--------------------------+
D |0000..............................0000|0000|    IPv4 address     |
D +--------------------------------------+----+---------------------+
a So `::a.b.c.d` would be an IPv4-compatible IPv6 address representing the IPv4 address `a.b.c.d`.
j To convert from an IPv4 address to an IPv4-compatible IPv6 address, use [`Ipv4Addr::to_ipv6_compatible`].
d Use [`Ipv6Addr::to_ipv4`] to convert an IPv4-compatible IPv6 address to the canonical IPv4 address.
_ [IETF RFC 4291 Section 2.5.5.1]: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4291#section-2.5.5.1
 ### IPv4-Mapped IPv6 Addresses
K IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses are defined in [IETF RFC 4291 Section 2.5.5.2].
J The RFC describes the format of an "IPv4-Mapped IPv6 address" as follows:
D |0000..............................0000|FFFF|    IPv4 address     |
b So `::ffff:a.b.c.d` would be an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address representing the IPv4 address `a.b.c.d`.
b To convert from an IPv4 address to an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address, use [`Ipv4Addr::to_ipv6_mapped`].
` Use [`Ipv6Addr::to_ipv4`] to convert an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address to the canonical IPv4 address.
S Note that this will also convert the IPv6 loopback address `::1` to `0.0.0.1`. Use
_ [IETF RFC 4291 Section 2.5.5.2]: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4291#section-2.5.5.2

< A marker trait which represents "panic safe" types in Rust.
M This trait is implemented by default for many types and behaves similarly in
N terms of inference of implementation to the [`Send`] and [`Sync`] traits. The
S purpose of this trait is to encode what types are safe to cross a [`catch_unwind`]
( boundary with no fear of unwind safety.
 ## What is unwind safety?
E In Rust a function can "return" early if it either panics or calls a
L function which transitively panics. This sort of control flow is not always
F anticipated, and has the possibility of causing subtle bugs through a
( combination of two critical components:
F 1. A data structure is in a temporarily invalid state when the thread
    panics.
1 2. This broken invariant is then later observed.
J Typically in Rust, it is difficult to perform step (2) because catching a
J panic involves either spawning a thread (which in turn makes it difficult
Q to later witness broken invariants) or using the `catch_unwind` function in this
N module. Additionally, even if an invariant is witnessed, it typically isn't a
N problem in Rust because there are no uninitialized values (like in C or C++).
J It is possible, however, for **logical** invariants to be broken in Rust,
N which can end up causing behavioral bugs. Another key aspect of unwind safety
I in Rust is that, in the absence of `unsafe` code, a panic cannot lead to
 memory unsafety.
N That was a bit of a whirlwind tour of unwind safety, but for more information
N about unwind safety and how it applies to Rust, see an [associated RFC][rfc].
X [rfc]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/1236-stabilize-catch-panic.md
 ## What is `UnwindSafe`?
G Now that we've got an idea of what unwind safety is in Rust, it's also
L important to understand what this trait represents. As mentioned above, one
P way to witness broken invariants is through the `catch_unwind` function in this
J module as it allows catching a panic and then re-using the environment of
 the closure.
I Simply put, a type `T` implements `UnwindSafe` if it cannot easily allow
L witnessing a broken invariant through the use of `catch_unwind` (catching a
L panic). This trait is an auto trait, so it is automatically implemented for
K many types, and it is also structurally composed (e.g., a struct is unwind
0 safe if all of its components are unwind safe).
L Note, however, that this is not an unsafe trait, so there is not a succinct
K contract that this trait is providing. Instead it is intended as more of a
L "speed bump" to alert users of `catch_unwind` that broken invariants may be
, witnessed and may need to be accounted for.
  ## Who implements `UnwindSafe`?
H Types such as `&mut T` and `&RefCell<T>` are examples which are **not**
L unwind safe. The general idea is that any mutable state which can be shared
P across `catch_unwind` is not unwind safe by default. This is because it is very
L easy to witness a broken invariant outside of `catch_unwind` as the data is
 simply accessed as usual.
H Types like `&Mutex<T>`, however, are unwind safe because they implement
J poisoning by default. They still allow witnessing a broken invariant, but
7 they already provide their own "speed bumps" to do so.
% ## When should `UnwindSafe` be used?
P It is not intended that most types or functions need to worry about this trait.
K It is only used as a bound on the `catch_unwind` function and as mentioned
@ above, the lack of `unsafe` means it is mostly an advisory. The
J [`AssertUnwindSafe`] wrapper struct can be used to force this trait to be
D implemented for any closed over variables passed to `catch_unwind`.

+ A pointer which pins its pointee in place.
Z [`Pin`] is a wrapper around some kind of pointer `Ptr` which makes that pointer "pin" its
^ pointee value in place, thus preventing the value referenced by that pointer from being moved
Q or otherwise invalidated at that place in memory unless it implements [`Unpin`].
S *See the [`pin` module] documentation for a more thorough exploration of pinning.*
$ ## Pinning values with [`Pin<Ptr>`]
\ will not be *moved* or [otherwise invalidated][subtle-details]. If the pointee value's type
\ implements [`Unpin`], we are free to disregard these requirements entirely and can wrap any
] pointer to that value in [`Pin`] directly via [`Pin::new`]. If the pointee value's type does
^ not implement [`Unpin`], then Rust will not let us use the [`Pin::new`] function directly and
Y we'll need to construct a [`Pin`]-wrapped pointer in one of the more specialized manners
 discussed below.
Y We call such a [`Pin`]-wrapped pointer a **pinning pointer** (or pinning ref, or pinning
\ [`Box`], etc.) because its existence is the thing that is pinning the underlying pointee in
\ place: it is the metaphorical "pin" securing the data in place on the pinboard (in memory).
^ It is important to stress that the thing in the [`Pin`] is not the value which we want to pin
] itself, but rather a pointer to that value! A [`Pin<Ptr>`] does not pin the `Ptr` but rather
# the pointer's ***pointee** value*.
\ The most common set of types which require pinning related guarantees for soundness are the
T compiler-generated state machines that implement [`Future`] for the return value of
] `async fn`s. These compiler-generated [`Future`]s may contain self-referential pointers, one
Y of the most common use cases for [`Pin`]. More details on this point are provided in the
^ [`pin` module] docs, but suffice it to say they require the guarantees provided by pinning to
 be implemented soundly.
W This requirement for the implementation of `async fn`s means that the [`Future`] trait
_ requires all calls to [`poll`] to use a <code>self: [Pin]\<&mut Self></code> parameter instead
] of the usual `&mut self`. Therefore, when manually polling a future, you will need to pin it
 first.
V You may notice that `async fn`-sourced [`Future`]s are only a small percentage of all
[ [`Future`]s that exist, yet we had to modify the signature of [`poll`] for all [`Future`]s
[ to accommodate them. This is unfortunate, but there is a way that the language attempts to
O alleviate the extra friction that this API choice incurs: the [`Unpin`] trait.
V The vast majority of Rust types have no reason to ever care about being pinned. These
X types implement the [`Unpin`] trait, which entirely opts all values of that type out of
` pinning-related guarantees. For values of these types, pinning a value by pointing to it with a
) [`Pin<Ptr>`] will have no actual effect.
\ The reason this distinction exists is exactly to allow APIs like [`Future::poll`] to take a
\ [`Pin<Ptr>`] as an argument for all types while only forcing [`Future`] types that actually
\ care about pinning guarantees pay the ergonomics cost. For the majority of [`Future`] types
[ that don't have a reason to care about being pinned and therefore implement [`Unpin`], the
\ <code>[Pin]\<&mut Self></code> will act exactly like a regular `&mut Self`, allowing direct
` access to the underlying value. Only types that *don't* implement [`Unpin`] will be restricted.
8 ### Pinning a value of a type that implements [`Unpin`]
\ If the type of the value you need to "pin" implements [`Unpin`], you can trivially wrap any
< pointer to that value in a [`Pin`] by calling [`Pin::new`].
4 // Create a value of a type that implements `Unpin`
. let mut unpin_future = std::future::ready(5);
P // Pin it by creating a pinning mutable reference to it (ready to be `poll`ed!)
G let my_pinned_unpin_future: Pin<&mut _> = Pin::new(&mut unpin_future);
% ### Pinning a value inside a [`Box`]
^ The simplest and most flexible way to pin a value that does not implement [`Unpin`] is to put
_ that value inside a [`Box`] and then turn that [`Box`] into a "pinning [`Box`]" by wrapping it
Y in a [`Pin`]. You can do both of these in a single step using [`Box::pin`]. Let's see an
] example of using this flow to pin a [`Future`] returned from calling an `async fn`, a common
 use case as described above.
" async fn add_one(x: u32) -> u32 {
0 // Call the async function to get a future back
 let fut = add_one(42);
' // Pin the future inside a pinning box
- let pinned_fut: Pin<Box<_>> = Box::pin(fut);
` If you have a value which is already boxed, for example a [`Box<dyn Future>`][Box], you can pin
K that value in-place at its current memory address using [`Box::into_pin`].
< fn boxed_add_one(x: u32) -> Box<dyn Future<Output = u32>> {
     Box::new(add_one(x))
# let boxed_fut = boxed_add_one(42);
* // Pin the future inside the existing box
8 let pinned_fut: Pin<Box<_>> = Box::into_pin(boxed_fut);
\ There are similar pinning methods offered on the other standard library smart pointer types
" as well, like [`Rc`] and [`Arc`].
0 ### Pinning a value on the stack using [`pin!`]
` There are some situations where it is desirable or even required (for example, in a `#[no_std]`
Y context where you don't have access to the standard library or allocation in general) to
Y pin a value which does not implement [`Unpin`] to its location on the stack. Doing so is
C possible using the [`pin!`] macro. See its documentation for more.

L Constructs a <code>[Pin]<[&mut] T></code>, by pinning a `value: T` locally.
N Unlike [`Box::pin`], this does not create a new heap allocation. As explained
; below, the element might still end up on the heap however.
M The local pinning performed by this macro is usually dubbed "stack"-pinning.
I Outside of `async` contexts locals do indeed get stored on the stack. In
K `async` functions or blocks however, any locals crossing an `.await` point
L are part of the state captured by the `Future`, and will use the storage of
J those. That storage can either be on the heap or on the stack. Therefore,
' local pinning is a more accurate term.
M If the type of the given value does not implement [`Unpin`], then this macro
J pins the value in memory in a way that prevents moves. On the other hand,
K if the type does implement [`Unpin`], <code>[Pin]<[&mut] T></code> behaves
3 like <code>[&mut] T</code>, and operations such as
M [`mem::replace()`][crate::mem::replace] or [`mem::take()`](crate::mem::take)
 will allow moves of the value.
G See [the `Unpin` section of the `pin` module][self#unpin] for details.

 ## Remarks
a Precisely because a value is pinned to local storage, the resulting <code>[Pin]<[&mut] T></code>
L reference ends up borrowing a local tied to that block: it can't escape it.
/ The following, for instance, fails to compile:
@ # use core::{marker::PhantomPinned as Foo, mem::drop as stuff};
 let x: Pin<&mut Foo> = {
4     let x: Pin<&mut Foo> = pin!(Foo { /* 
 */ });
 }; // <- Foo is dropped
) stuff(x); // Error: use of dropped value
* <details><summary>Error message</summary>
 ```console
5 error[E0716]: temporary value dropped while borrowed
   --> src/main.rs:9:28
 8  | let x: Pin<&mut Foo> = {
$    |     - borrow later stored here
9 9  |     let x: Pin<&mut Foo> = pin!(Foo { /* 
 */ });
r    |                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ creates a temporary value which is freed while still in use
 10 |     x
 11 | }; // <- Foo is dropped
=    | - temporary value is freed at the end of this statement
I    = note: consider using a `let` binding to create a longer lived value
 </details>
_ This makes [`pin!`] **unsuitable to pin values when intending to _return_ them**. Instead, the
] value is expected to be passed around _unpinned_ until the point where it is to be consumed,
S where it is then useful and even sensible to pin the value locally using [`pin!`].
R If you really need to return a pinned value, consider using [`Box::pin`] instead.
M On the other hand, local pinning using [`pin!`] is likely to be cheaper than
T pinning into a fresh heap allocation using [`Box::pin`]. Moreover, by virtue of not
Z requiring an allocator, [`pin!`] is the main non-`unsafe` `#![no_std]`-compatible [`Pin`]
 constructor.

 Atomic memory orderings
G Memory orderings specify the way atomic operations synchronize memory.
N In its weakest [`Ordering::Relaxed`], only the memory directly touched by the
X operation is synchronized. On the other hand, a store-load pair of [`Ordering::SeqCst`]
X operations synchronize other memory while additionally preserving a total order of such
 operations across all threads.
2 Rust's memory orderings are [the same as those of
? C++20](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/memory_order).

M A future represents an asynchronous computation, commonly obtained by use of
 [`async`].
M A future is a value that might not have finished computing yet. This kind of
M "asynchronous value" makes it possible for a thread to continue doing useful
7 work while it waits for the value to become available.
 # The `poll` method
K The core method of future, `poll`, *attempts* to resolve the future into a
L final value. This method does not block if the value is not ready. Instead,
H the current task is scheduled to be woken up when it's possible to make
H further progress by `poll`ing again. The `context` passed to the `poll`
L method can provide a [`Waker`], which is a handle for waking up the current
 task.
K When using a future, you generally won't call `poll` directly, but instead
 `.await` the value.
 [`Waker`]: crate::task::Waker
`{Self}` is not a future
` is not a future
* The type of value produced on completion.
= Attempts to resolve the future to a final value, registering
? the current task for wakeup if the value is not yet available.
 This function returns:
3 - [`Poll::Pending`] if the future is not ready yet
B - [`Poll::Ready(val)`] with the result `val` of this future if it
   finished successfully.
@ Once a future has finished, clients should not `poll` it again.
C When a future is not ready yet, `poll` returns `Poll::Pending` and
E stores a clone of the [`Waker`] copied from the current [`Context`].
@ This [`Waker`] is then woken once the future can make progress.
5 For example, a future waiting for a socket to become
> readable would call `.clone()` on the [`Waker`] and store it.
H When a signal arrives elsewhere indicating that the socket is readable,
B [`Waker::wake`] is called and the socket future's task is awoken.
F Once a task has been woken up, it should attempt to `poll` the future
3 again, which may or may not produce a final value.
C Note that on multiple calls to `poll`, only the [`Waker`] from the
B [`Context`] passed to the most recent call should be scheduled to
 receive a wakeup.
 # Runtime characteristics
D Futures alone are *inert*; they must be *actively* `poll`ed for the
D underlying computation to make progress, meaning that each time the
G current task is woken up, it should actively re-`poll` pending futures
" that it still has an interest in.
C Having said that, some Futures may represent a value that is being
D computed in a different task. In this case, the future's underlying
E computation is simply acting as a conduit for a value being computed
D by that other task, which will proceed independently of the Future.
M Futures of this kind are typically obtained when spawning a new task into an
 async runtime.
G The `poll` function should not be called repeatedly in a tight loop --
G instead, it should only be called when the future indicates that it is
J ready to make progress (by calling `wake()`). If you're familiar with the
I `poll(2)` or `select(2)` syscalls on Unix it's worth noting that futures
F typically do *not* suffer the same problems of "all wakeups must poll
, all events"; they are more like `epoll(4)`.
H An implementation of `poll` should strive to return quickly, and should
@ not block. Returning quickly prevents unnecessarily clogging up
D threads or event loops. If it is known ahead of time that a call to
D `poll` may end up taking a while, the work should be offloaded to a
D thread pool (or something similar) to ensure that `poll` can return
	 quickly.
H Once a future has completed (returned `Ready` from `poll`), calling its
F `poll` method again may panic, block forever, or cause other kinds of
F problems; the `Future` trait places no requirements on the effects of
C such a call. However, as the `poll` method is not marked `unsafe`,
" regardless of the future's state.
" [`Poll::Ready(val)`]: Poll::Ready
* [`Waker::wake`]: crate::task::Waker::wake
